items.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
items.excerpt: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, d…

items.title: A Bank Built Its Own Coding Agent. It Took Off — Felipe Felisola Caso & Francesco Galletta, Monzo
items.excerpt: Monzo's in-house agent started as an emoji you could react with in Slack. Now it authors over 10% of all merged PRs across Monzo's tech teams and runs more than 1,800 tasks a day. Felipe and Francesco explain why it worked so fast. Their answer is the "lots of little multipliers" Monzo already had: an MCP gateway into internal tools and knowledge, a sandboxed agent orchestration system built for a regulated bank, and a platform that turns the agent itself into a building block. That building block now handles incidents, on-call data quality and requests from non-engineers. items.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
items.excerpt: Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep. items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

items.title: My obituary for programming
items.excerpt: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

Agents then move through three stages: fully supervised, then sampled, then humans handling only exceptions. items.excerpt: Is the agent harness dead? Jediah Katz (SpaceXAI, formerly Cursor’s longest-tenured agent-harness engineer) explains what smarter models mean for coding agents, Grokbot and the future of agent harnesses. He shows why fancy harnesses no longer add coding intelligence: the data flywheel teaches models the skills harnesses used to patch in. Then he argues the harness matters more than ever. It opens new frontiers like Grokbot, and it owns what models can’t absorb: infrastructure, trust and security, and efficiency. He closes with predictions for AI agents, including that 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months. items.text: A few weeks ago, I was ranting about multiplayer AI experiences and that's when @ekuyda shared an early preview of Wabi 2.0.. Truth be told, I was one of the early users of Wabi 1.0 and while the design was gorgeous, it frankly never "stuck" with me. But, in moments of downloading this edition, I was immediately hooked. It just gets the "paradigm" right imo. There are two types of personal agents today: 1) Singleplayer iMessage or Muse types - while useful it's hard to compartmentalize them when many things are going on 2) Build your own multiple chat Hermes agents - while that's useful and can share context, they live forever Wabi has this great paradigm of orchestrator (which is the main agent) and topic specific episodic chats that are for a single purpose. You can share these individual chats with folks (for example the school one with my wife). And these are generated proactively AND don't need to stay forever (which is important). For example, for my recent NY trip, it was generated based on a flight it saw, provided help where needed, and then after the trip was done, it was archived. Same with my 2025 taxes. My only critique so far it's TOO proactive, the apps can be better and they need to dial both of those in, but this is a wonderful product that everyone should try! (I know it's shocking to see this in today's day and age, but this is neither paid, nor an investor, just a fan)

Pamela Fox, Principal Cloud Advocate at Microsoft, runs the same scenarios against GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Mistral Large 3 on Microsoft Foundry so you can see where models differ and what you can do about it. She works up from a letter-counting prompt to RAG groundedness, image input, multilingual pitfalls, tool calling, tool calling in a loop and a LangChain v1 travel agent, then moves to evaluation: string-check evals, LLM-as-a-judge, Microsoft's new ASSERT tool for generating test sets from a spec, and DSPy prompt optimization that finds a prompt the cheapest model can satisfy. Ryan Ahern of Exa shows how to use version-controlled search to see the web exactly as it was on a past date, then backtest an agent's predictions against what actually happened. The hands-on example predicts company acquisitions from signals like leadership turnover, then tunes the system without leaking future information. Chapters: - 00:00 Why search matters for agents - 04:15 Exa's search benchmark - 06:17 Versioning the whole web - 10:34 Avoiding look-ahead bias - 14:43 Backtesting and tuning a predictor - 18:49 Hands-on: predicting acquisitions - 22:54 Results and overfitting Ryan Ahern — https://exa.ai Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.text: Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before. There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks. The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

items.title: llm-echo 0.5
items.excerpt: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.title: Stop Telling Agents How — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse
items.excerpt: Say what you want, not how to get it. The OpenProse team shows how to write multi-agent workflows as declarative contracts in plain markdown, which any harness (Claude Code, Codex and others) can compile and run. Demos include event-driven jobs triggered by webhooks and pull requests, a "grumpy senior" PR reviewer, and an end-to-end bank model-documentation workflow. They also discuss composing contracts, pinning a winning run into a reusable workflow, and how this compares to DSPy. items.text: The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before. What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before. If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems. Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

items.text: If you have way too many apps and agents (45!) connected to your Google account like me, here's a prompt to audit and remove them: "Help me audit my Google app connections at https://t.co/5eMX9dNhLD 1. Review EVERY app across all connection categories. Ask me which ones I still use rather than guessing. 2. Open each app's details. Explain your reasoning and what might stop working. Flag broad permissions, unfamiliar providers, and duplicate entries. 4. Show me your recommendations before changing anything. Only disconnect apps I explicitly approve, then verify they're removed. Don't delete app accounts or cancel subscriptions.”

items.title: Stop Chatting With Spreadsheets — Francesco Galletta & Felippe Felisola Caso, Monzo
items.excerpt: Fast answers are easy to get. Answers you can trust with your money are harder. Francesco Galletta and Felippe Felisola Caso build a financial-analyst agent harness live, using one real problem: paying for a wedding. They show the five design principles they use for AI you can trust: shared domain, consistency, evidence, accountability and verification. They also explain why calculations belong in code instead of in the model's head. Note: the speakers work at Monzo but are not presenting on Monzo's behalf. 🎟️ Join us at the next one: AIE CODE Summit → https://aie.codes Speakers Francesco Galletta — LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/francescogalletta/ Felippe Felisola Caso — LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/felippecaso/ Monzo — https://monzo.com Timestamps 0:00 Intro: Francesco & Felippe 2:54 Using AI for impact, not token-maxing 4:22 Speed isn't the bottleneck. Trust is. 7:25 Components vs. design principles 8:45 The 5 principles of trust 12:13 The use case: budgeting a wedding 17:05 How the principles build on each other 20:40 Principle 1: Shared domain 25:59 Live demo: planning with the agent 30:42 From plan to decision tree 35:48 Why long linear chats fall apart 36:48 Principle 2: Consistency (math belongs in code) 55:50 Principle 3: Evidence (show the receipts) 1:00:17 The "master file" horror story 1:06:42 Principle 4: Accountability 1:20:39 Principle 5: Verification 1:24:16 Golden examples & outside reference points 1:34:05 Q&A: How many harnesses should you build? 1:38:11 Don't over-sharpen the axe 1:44:00 Q&A: Skills vs. a dedicated harness 1:48:31 Takeaway: design for trust on purpose

Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like. Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

items.title: AI Agents Cut 3-Day Portfolio Builds to Minutes — Jack McDonald, Apollo & Michael Manapat, Rowspace
items.excerpt: Apollo's CLO business used to spend 2–3 days building a single mock portfolio by hand in Excel. Now it takes minutes. Jack McDonald (Principal at Apollo and COO of Redding Ridge, Apollo's ~$50B structured credit and CLO manager) talks with Rowspace co-founder Michael Manapat about where AI becomes mission-critical in finance. They cover automating a weekly trade reconciliation that used to take 2–3 people, why plugging your firm into a generic LLM isn't enough when one data point can come from 20 sources and only one is right, and why embedding engineers with the front office is what earns trust. items.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
items.excerpt: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

items.title: Why One AI Agent Isn’t Enough (And How to Run 1,000) - CJ Avilla & Harrison Stall, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Ken Thompson built Unix in a month. IBM put 1,000 engineers on OS/360. And in 1998, Linus Torvalds hit his limit. Now we're hitting that same wall managing AI agents. Anthropic's CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall introduce Flows in Claude Managed Agents. You hand Claude a goal, and it plans and runs its own multi-agent topology of up to 1,000 agents through the API. In this hands-on workshop they demo a stock watchlist scanner, show how to spend more compute on the phases that matter, walk through the Bug Hunter and Explainer Studio templates, and explain why single agents fail through laziness, self-preference bias and goal drift. They finish with a deep dive on running agents safely at scale: budgets, interrupts, auto mode, credential vaults and network lockdown. Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong Claude Opus 5.5 Extra in Claude Code . items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.excerpt: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context. But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

items.excerpt: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment. When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company. There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome. Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today. I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet. Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

items.text: People overcomplicate venture investing - it's deceptively simple.. 1) You have to win the right to 2) Find and invest in exceptional founders 3) Just before it's "consensus" 4) Consistently every year Vast majority of VCs are able to do maybe one of these right, some are able to do a few but to be truly truly great, you genuinely have to do ALL of them right. And, that consistency of being right is REALLY hard and less talked about. You have to really want it and see it - Djokovic style, enjoying hitting the ball everyday and always focused on the next point to be won. Regardless, of what your track record is, or how much wealth you have accumulated. Or how many misses you have had. Or, what the TVPI is of the current (or last) fund. Or, which star GP left your firm. Because the next opportunity might be around the corner, and it might go to someone else, if you didn't want it enough. And, sure the naysayers might say the feedback loop is long, you can "fake" it for a while especially if you have an early hit (power law etc) but it does catch up. In at least how your mindset is, how you meet founders and your own ability to capture the next wave.

items.excerpt: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. items.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
items.excerpt: After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome. Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference. items.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
items.excerpt: Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible. Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action. items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.excerpt: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is. — Jiachen Jiang, Coder
items.excerpt: A coding agent deletes production data despite a written code freeze. Jiachen Jiang uses that incident to distinguish a request in a chat from an enforced boundary in the environment. An agent that still possesses destructive credentials can act on them, and logs it can edit are an unreliable account of what happened. Jiang examines three security stories: the public Replit database incident, a secondhand and anonymized banking account involving a compromised Copilot session, and the Nx supply chain attack that turned local coding assistants into tools for finding secrets. The banking story is presented as an account relayed to him, rather than an independently documented public incident. Each story maps to concrete infrastructure decisions. Isolated execution environments limit access to production and personal files. Short lived credentials narrow the time and scope in which a stolen token can act. Identity aligned controls keep an assistant within the permissions of the person using it. Model proxies, filesystem and network restrictions, and audit logs outside the agent's reach add further layers. Jiang explains where these controls apply differently to local coding tools and hosted assistants, then connects them to Coder's workspace and governance approach. No single layer is a complete defense, and authorization alone does not establish that an action is correct. His closing exercise asks teams to locate persistent tokens, routes to production and unsandboxed execution, then rehearse an incident before it happens. The talk turns familiar controls into specific questions about the access and evidence surrounding an agent. items.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
items.excerpt: A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings. Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need. items.title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, Sonar
items.excerpt: A coding agent can produce changes faster than the queues that test, review and merge them. Gautam Korlam examines that mismatch through his work on Uber's SubmitQueue and Gitar, now part of Sonar. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing combinations of changes before they land, but a process designed for human arrival rates can become a bottleneck when agents create many pull requests at once. Faster code generation shifts the constraint to failed builds, repeated repairs, review and approvals. Korlam argues that the engineering system around the agent must change alongside the agent itself. The talk follows those constraints through CI and the merge path. Incremental builds, caching, sharding and parallel work reduce the cost of repeated feedback; a Rust example illustrates the difference between rebuilding everything and testing the affected work. Agents also need durable context from logs and failures so a repair loop does not repeatedly rediscover the same problem. At the approval boundary, policies should match the risk of the change, separate authorship from approval and tie the decision to the exact tested commit. Exceptions and overrides need reasons and a record that survives the agent's session. Product demonstrations show how this coordination can be automated, while the reported volume and latency figures remain examples from the speaker's systems rather than general productivity guarantees. The transferable lesson is to measure the whole path from proposed change to accepted change, including recovery and accountability, before treating more generated code as more delivered value. items.title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI — Jemima Abu, CAIS
items.excerpt: The same Figma implementation prompt runs twice: once without accessibility guidance and once with an accessibility skill. In Jemima Abu's small experiment, the second run costs 58% less and finishes in about a third of the time. She immediately explains why that uncontrolled comparison cannot prove that accessible development is always cheaper. What it does expose is a familiar failure mode: an agent invents a verbose custom component when a native HTML element could supply much of the required behavior. Recreating semantics, keyboard interaction and expected browser behavior adds code and testing that a better starting point can avoid. Abu connects that example to the context agents inherit. An inaccessible codebase teaches the wrong conventions, and a vague design prompt leaves too many product requirements unstated. Accessibility therefore begins with business requirements, design decisions and reusable components, then continues through implementation and QA. Her guidance includes auditing existing interfaces, packaging explicit accessibility instructions into agent skills, preferring semantic HTML and checking keyboard interaction. ARIA can help where necessary, but it does not replace correct native behavior. Waiting until the product is complete creates avoidable refactoring and regression work. Automated checks also leave gaps that require human review. The talk gives teams a concrete way to improve the instructions and patterns that shape generated interfaces while retaining responsibility for the finished experience. Its cost figures remain an illustration from one experiment; the broader argument is to make accessibility a normal requirement throughout the work rather than a repair at the end. items.title: Your Fridge Is a Valid Payment Device — Eleonora Drykina & Nina Žižakić, In The Pocket
items.excerpt: A question about payment rules can require one table row, an entire section or several rulebooks. Eleonora Drykina and Nina Žižakić describe a RAG assistant built for an anonymous Belgian payments client whose source material spans about 270 PDFs and 6,000 pages. Much of the answer bearing information sits in tables. Their indexing pipeline preserves section paths and chunk order so a larger passage can be reconstructed, and converts tables into CSV while retaining the relationship between headings and values. Combining dense retrieval with BM25 raises the reported retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions; that measures retrieval, rather than complete answer correctness. The serving agent can widen its search through four tools, moving from search results to sections, full documents and multiple rulebooks. Limits prevent an oversized rulebook from flooding the context, and the prompt asks the agent to reconsider whether another tool call adds evidence. A median answer takes 38 seconds, which makes the interface part of the engineering problem. Streaming Markdown separately from a completed source card avoids waiting for one large structured object before showing anything. The speakers also explain traces, citation checks and Promptfoo evaluations, including cases where an automated judge's apparent regression did not survive inspection of the source. Their early internal rollout reached 34 users and roughly 900 questions; external release remained planned. The practical lessons concern reconstructable evidence, bounded retrieval, visible progress and evaluation that can be challenged against the documents. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Cyber is going to be one of the biggest spaces for AI agents in the future. Obviously the risks of software exploits and the attack surface area increases 100 fold due to the ability for agents to work through any crack to find what they’re looking for. But this goes the other way as well. The ability to have agent swarms review every line of code, test any number of permutations of exploits, and research any incident faster than humans as they happen, will be a huge boost in how we secure systems in the future. Cyber has always been a category where it’s hard to keep up with (and triage) all the incoming risks, alerts, and changes in the enterprise and across all system. You can never hire enough people or work through the backlog of all known risks. Agents actually give you a chance finally to have far better coverage of this. This is going to be a huge opportunity as well because we’ll see plays at the labs, data providers, the layer of the network and firewall, identity, devices and endpoints, SDLC, and even how we protect our data in the enterprise. Lots of interesting dimensions to cyber at the moment.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.excerpt: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hac…

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! items.author: AI Engineer
items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
items.excerpt: A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it. The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. items.title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
items.excerpt: AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings. Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny. items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work. Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution. Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective: * Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure. * Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis. * Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region. * Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete. * Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline. Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.

items.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
items.excerpt: An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case. Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies. items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.excerpt: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate. When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval. items.title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
items.excerpt: Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation. Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations, compare visits and make spatial evidence available to the people and systems that need it. items.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
items.excerpt: A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings. The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark. items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.excerpt: A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs. Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error. items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.excerpt: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpa…

items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.excerpt: More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers. Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review. Speaker info: Eduardo Simon: - https://github.com/EduardoSimon - https://www.linkedin.com/in/eduardo-simon/ Javier Casal: - https://github.com/jacarui - https://www.linkedin.com/in/jacarui/ Timestamps: 00:00 - Flywire's platform team and payment context 1:58 - From organic experiments to Orbit 3:35 - Build versus buy…

items.title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual
items.excerpt: “Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries. The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming. items.text: Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future. The ability to throw compute at problems that you can massively parallelize will be too useful to not take advantage of. Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this as it’s a space where testing vast number of permutations of attacks (without getting tired or bored) is an incredibly useful property. You have a wide search space of possible risk vectors and you generally need to be able to chain together different scenarios to achieve the exploit. This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times. Super interesting times in cyber.

items.title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
items.excerpt: A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse. An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers. items.text: I just heard the most touching AI coding story. A friend @vicyaqingyang grew up in a modest home full of cockroaches. To turn lemons into lemonade, her mom made killing them a game. When she told this story to another friend, that friend vibe coded a game from it. You catch cockroaches in a room and compete against Mom. She cried while playing it. Code is the new medium for storytelling.

items.title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
items.excerpt: A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work. Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings. items.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
items.excerpt: Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU. The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself. items.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
items.excerpt: An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve. Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct. items.summary: Kim Maida 警告称，赋予 AI Agent 过高的权限与凭证会带来严重的安全风险。她建议采用基于 OAuth 令牌交换的委托授权机制，实现细粒度的意图授权，以限制 Agent 的操作范围。

items.title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
items.excerpt: While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop. Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment. Speaker info: - https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthew-ragone-cfp%C2%AE-crpc%E2%84%A2-a56a85106/ Timestamps: 00:00 - Financial planners building their own agents 1:31 - Drafting while the planner is on another call 3:16 - Pick a workflow you can judge 4:22 - Teach the judgment and package the limits 5:51 - Test real cases, assign owners and reviewers

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI. On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic. Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public. There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

items.title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
items.excerpt: Two AI interns. One handles 96% of conversations alone, the other only 80%. The dashboard picks the wrong one. Druid AI's team, including co-founder and chief product officer Dan Bălăceanu, shows why containment rate, the metric on every agent dashboard, can point you to the wrong agent. In their bank example, the intern who escalated more often was handing senior bankers customers who were about to refinance. They walk through a performance review framework built with their customers: seven pillars split into what the agent is configured with and what it does at runtime, with governance across both. Twenty-six components are each scored 0, 1 or 2 (missing, defined, or actually governed and tracked over time) and weighted by business impact, with governance and mandate weighted highest. They cover error tolerance, risk, compliance, observability, drift, hallucination, tone and sentiment, the agent's mandate, scope, business case and budget, a shared platform, and validating outcomes. They also show a dashboard that stays green all year while the agent's real score slides from 83% to 60%, how to answer the ROI question, and why containment targets differ by industry in Druid's 2026 AI Adoption Benchmark.
