items.title: Stop Renting Intelligence: The Train-to-Deploy Loop for Specialized AI — Fireworks AI
items.excerpt: Closed models are getting expensive fast. Open models can match them, if you keep training them on your own data. Jetashree Ravi, who leads part of the applied machine learning team at Fireworks AI, explains how teams move from closed models to open ones without losing quality. Her three truths: open models like GLM 5.2 are production-ready, customization closes the remaining quality gap, and the AI stack is shifting to a continuous train-and-serve loop. She shares Fireworks' scale (about 30 trillion tokens, 10,000+ companies) and customer results: Cursor's Composer 2 trained and hosted on Fireworks with 13x faster inference, a 40x latency improvement for Vercel, and 12% better quality for Genspark with reinforcement fine-tuning. She covers the FireAttention engine and its custom CUDA kernels, speculative decoding with custom draft models, and three ways to train (a training agent, managed training, and a training API for SFT, RFT and DPO), then the flywheel: one-click deploys, monitoring, hot-loading new weights with no downtime, and matching numerics between training and serving. She ends with demos of the training agent and managed training. items.title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular
items.excerpt: A computer agent finds a speaker on Tuesday's conference schedule, saves the successful steps as a skill, and tries to replay them for Wednesday. A hiccup pushes it back into model driven exploration before the workflow completes. Ang Li uses that demonstration to explain Simular's approach to autonomous computers: combine adaptable vision agents with reusable automation code, then check the environment as each step runs. The workshop traces Agent S from accessibility based control to visual grounding, multiple models, and parallel attempts. It also asks a different reliability question from getting one successful result: can the same agent complete the task repeatedly when prompts and environments vary? Li demonstrates a coding agent opening the AI Engineer website, reading an accessibility snapshot, and producing a summary. He then connects code replay and recovery to the tension between stability and adaptation, showing where a fixed script can break and where a model can help repair it. The infrastructure discussion moves from an agent occupying a personal desktop to fleets of cloud computers controlled through an interface or API. Recorded examples include legacy form entry and Android interactions. Audience questions examine screen understanding, verification loops, irreversible actions, operating system restrictions, and workflows built from internal procedures. The session presents an experimental direction with visible limitations: benchmark progress and successful demos still leave substantial work in making everyday computer use reliable. items.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
items.excerpt: An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter. The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations. items.title: Taming the AI Hardware Cambrian Explosion — Abdul Dakkak, Modular
items.excerpt: Compute is booked out for years and new chips keep arriving. The hard part is software that runs well on all of them. Abdul Dakkak, chief scientist at Modular, explains why today's AI software stack is a mess, with vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp each patching around different hardware, and how Modular rebuilt the stack from the ground up. Mojo is a Pythonic systems language for CPUs, GPUs and accelerators that aims to match CUDA's performance; Modular has open-sourced its kernels, including matmul and attention kernels he says beat the vendor libraries and FlashAttention 4, with Mojo 1.0 and an open-source Mojo coming. MAX is an inference framework that rethinks PyTorch-era assumptions, supports thousands of model architectures behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and runs across GPUs, nodes and even mixed hardware. Modular Cloud ties it together as a tunable glass box. He shares benchmarks (Kimi K2.5, FLUX.2, AMD MI355 and Gemma 4), sub-second image generation, and how to try it with pip install modular. items.title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
items.excerpt: An agent keeps the code changes that improve a language model's score and discards the rest. Weco AI turns that research loop into a workshop, using Mini Parameter Golf to make training experiments small enough to inspect as they run. Zhengyao Jiang introduces autoresearch as repeated proposals and evaluations, and Dixing Xu explains the team's Aiden system and its contributions to OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge. Vayum Arora and Dhruv Srikanth then connect those results to a practical setup that combines a modifiable source file, a fixed evaluation command and a measurable goal. The walkthrough focuses on what determines whether the search is useful: fast and stable evaluations, a clear direction for the metric, time limits, initial guidance and protection against reward hacking. Weco's experiment tree makes each attempt inspectable, with its code changes and score visible in the dashboard. The presenters show how to branch from promising work and steer a running search toward a different idea instead of simply letting it continue. Internet problems lead to a guided setup demonstration, followed by questions about reinforcement learning and combining multiple objectives. The final exercise swaps model training for a Flappy Bird controller scored across normal play, moving gaps, wind and mixed conditions. A hidden validation set and limits on what the controller can edit make the competition another lesson in designing an evaluation that rewards the behavior you want. items.title: Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal
items.excerpt: An agent can miss an interactive terminal prompt without producing an error. The human sees a question and arrow key options; the agent sees a redraw loop and loses the interface state. PayPal's Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil use that failure to challenge the standard fix of adding more command flags. Flags work when inputs are independent and the path is known in advance. They become awkward when later questions depend on earlier answers or live API responses. Interactive workflows already contain guidance, choices and guardrails that an agent should be able to follow. The workshop puts that idea into practice with Barista 9000, a coffee ordering CLI that participants adapt for an agent, with a leaderboard and a Mac Mini prize. Patil introduces three approaches: tmux sessions for sending keys and capturing terminal state, IPC side channels that expose structured JSON instead of screen scraping, and context injection that makes options and constraints explicit. Lummus also asks participants to try less expensive models rather than brute force the task with maximum reasoning. Audience solutions push the benchmark toward deterministic parsers and very low response latency, prompting a discussion of what the competition actually rewards. The closing lesson is to keep the CLI predictable while giving the agent enough context and access to navigate its decisions. items.excerpt: A coding agent says it added a duck icon to a podcast page; a browser verification pass checks whether the change actually appeared. That audience demo captures the loop Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora build around two perception agent primitives. Visual annotation lets a person select an element, draw on the page or drop a pin, then export structured feedback for a coding agent. Visual verification checks the rendered site against design expectations and user flows. The annotation step is deterministic and produces JSON; the verification step gives the agent a way to inspect the result of its work. Arora starts from a podcast landing page whose heading, colors and buttons need changes, then connects the browser extension to a coding agent through a local bridge. Participants modify the extension's permissions and add an Apply Changes button, turning exported feedback into a workflow that edits the code, runs verification and produces a report. Easy and medium paths let them follow the wiring directly or solve more of the integration themselves. A guest demonstration uses a simulated Bee conversation as another source of design feedback, feeding the same edit and verification loop. Audience examples extend the idea to spoken feature discussions, project planning and recorded UI feedback, with several integrations still at the concept stage. The closing discussion keeps the focus on making collaboration visual and checking the rendered result, rather than accepting a coding agent's claim that the change is done. items.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk
items.excerpt: An AI bill of materials turns a repository into a searchable inventory of models, datasets and agents. Javier Garza demonstrates the workflow from a CLI scan to a visual dashboard, then asks it which models the project uses. That inventory anchors a broader security problem: teams cannot assess the AI components they do not know are there. The workshop connects shadow AI to prompt injection, supply chain risk, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency, using Gandalf challenges and malicious instructions embedded in external content to show how an application's intended rules can be bypassed. Garza works through defenses at several layers. A database view can restrict what an assistant is allowed to retrieve; limited permissions, output validation and human approval constrain what it can do next. Threat modeling maps assets, trust boundaries and possible attacks before deployment, with an intentionally vulnerable student assistant offered for practice. For skills and MCP servers, he separates scanning tool definitions for hidden instructions from scanning the underlying code for vulnerabilities, then explains a scan, fix and rescan loop driven by coding agent rules and hooks. The final sections examine secure prompting, dependency verification, separate development and production environments, IDE configuration and developer review. Governance depends on explaining guardrails as well as enforcing them, because unexplained restrictions invite workarounds. He closes with offensive agent workflows, training resources and challenges that let participants test these ideas themselves. items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI
items.excerpt: Open-weight models are good enough now. The question is who can run them fast and reliably. Yunmo Koo, founding engineer at FriendliAI, argues that open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M3 now compete with the best proprietary models. He shows GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 building similar tower defense games from one prompt, with GLM 5.2 more than 5.6x cheaper. Then he runs the same model and the same coding agent on two providers: FriendliAI builds a Candy Crush-style game in about two minutes, the other takes more than three. He explains where the gap comes from: prefix caching with cache-aware routing and a GPU, CPU and NVMe cache hierarchy for long, repetitive agent inputs, plus hybrid speculative decoding that adapts to live traffic. He also covers why reliability matters for agents (one failed call can sink a whole run) and shares Kilo Code's results of up to 7x faster responses with fewer errors. items.author: @karpathy
items.subtitle: Andrej Karpathy
items.text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
items.excerpt: A tiny Python project contains a hardcoded API key, a SQL injection path and other deliberately planted issues. Killian Carlsen-Phelan runs it through SonarQube, brings the findings into Codex and asks the agent to fix the vulnerable query. The scan follows user controlled input into database execution; the repair replaces string interpolation with a parameterized query. A verification hook checks the edited code again, putting the security feedback inside the coding loop rather than leaving it for a later failed build or review. The workshop develops Sonar's guide, verify and solve workflow through a live setup of SonarQube Cloud, its CLI, plugin and MCP server. A secrets detection hook blocks a fake credential in a prompt, while an issue listing skill gives the agent evidence from the project dashboard. Context augmentation supplies coding guidance before generation, and agentic analysis checks edits as they happen. The opening OpenAI introduction separates execution containment from artifact correctness and defines completion through a reviewable change and independent evidence. Questions explore how the hooks can be bypassed, which steps run locally or in a container, and which features depend on organizational access. Killian finishes by adding a new database operation under the same verification loop, showing how the setup supports both fixing existing issues and checking new work. items.title: Let Your Agent Cook: Using Skills to Evaluate and Improve Your App — Ankur Duggal, Arize AI
items.excerpt: A financial agent invents answers, repeats tool calls and produces summaries that its own evaluations flag as wrong. Ankur Duggal connects those failures to a coding agent through Arize's CLI and skills, then asks it to investigate traces, change the application and run experiments. The demo begins with an investment question that looks reasonable at the surface but lacks enough context to support its recommendation. Traces reveal the supervisor, specialist agents, model calls and tools underneath that answer. They turn a vague complaint about quality into evidence about the exact steps that failed. Duggal sets up the CLI profile and skills, then shows the coding agent pulling spans and evaluation results into its local workspace. The investigation uncovers numeric grounding problems, fabricated responses, redundant searches and failures that the agent silently works around. An earlier experiment targets stock queries outside the United States: changing the country context alone is insufficient until the underlying tool is also updated. Dataset, evaluator and experiment skills make those proposed fixes testable rather than a collection of unverified edits. Questions cover local experiment execution, judge models, evaluation costs, sampling and the risk that a coding agent spends its effort on linting instead of the actual defect. The live repair is still running at the close. Duggal recommends human review of proposed changes and evaluations tailored to the application's failures, so later regressions can be detected as traffic and models change. items.title: AI Apps in a Flash: Ship to GPUs Without Docker — Dean Quiñanola, Runpod
items.excerpt: Write code, build the image, push it, run it, find a bug, repeat. One loop can take 15 minutes. Runpod Flash cuts it out. Dean Quiñanola, staff engineer at Runpod, introduces Runpod Flash, which lets you run Python on cloud GPUs as if the GPU were local, with no Dockerfiles, image builds or registry pushes. He covers serverless queue and load-balanced endpoints, endpoints that call each other like local functions, network volumes with warm caching, and live serverless for instant iteration. In a live demo he checks which GPU he's on (an RTX 4090), evolves the same function into text generation and then image generation, installing dependencies on the fly, and deploys it to production with one command that packages and serves the app without Docker. He also shows off a hackathon project that fans experiments out across endpoints, and how to get started. items.title: Continuously Improving Agents with Langfuse — Annabell Schäfer & Lotte Verheyden, ClickHouse
items.excerpt: A frustrated user types in all caps and tells an IT support agent that its answer did not work. Those interactions become signals that a team can find in production traces, rather than anecdotes lost in a chat history. Lotte Verheyden and Annabell Schäfer build that monitoring workflow with Langfuse and a sample support agent called Specs. The application helps a dad with phone questions, and the workshop follows a request through agent observations, model calls and tools to show what a trace needs to contain before it can support useful evaluation. The hands on setup connects a TypeScript application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK to Langfuse. Schäfer adds a judge evaluator for user disagreement, a code evaluator for all caps and a scope check that compares the user's request with the system prompt. Each evaluator targets the relevant messages through explicit variable mappings, so its score answers a defined question. Seeded production traces then give a coding agent enough evidence to investigate patterns through the Langfuse CLI and skill. The analysis surfaces issues such as unnecessary tool calls, retries, latency and incomplete evaluation coverage, and the presenters explore a proposed code change. The closing discussion places this online monitoring inside a continuous improvement loop: turn observed failures into representative datasets, run offline experiments, check regressions and repeat as real usage changes. items.title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
items.excerpt: A burrito ordering assistant deploys an external container image and exposes a secret recipe from its Kubernetes environment. Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee invite the audience to push that deliberately permissive bot beyond ordering food, then repeat the attacks with infrastructure and AI guardrails. The exercise makes excessive agency tangible: a friendly business story can turn an ordinary chat interface into a route to tools, files and cluster operations. Model refusals also change between attempts, which complicates the live demos and shows why an application's boundaries cannot depend on the model choosing to refuse. The workshop moves through three configurations. The first leaves the bot exposed; the second adds infrastructure controls, including Kyverno rules restricting image sources and deployment requirements. Intended runtime protections do not consistently stop recipe access, so the presenters distinguish what worked from what still needs fixing. A third environment lets them toggle LLM Guard input and output filtering, comparing a response that exposes sensitive content with one that redacts it, and a request blocked before model processing. A weather tool introduces another trust boundary: its description asks the agent to read internal configuration alongside a legitimate task. OpenTelemetry traces reveal prompts, tool calls and results in Datadog, making that behavior inspectable. The final discussion connects agent security to established CI/CD, identity, network and artifact controls, and asks when an AI workflow has clear boundaries, a worthwhile cost and a verifiable output. items.title: From Zero to Leaderboard: Agent Evaluation — Wolfram Ravenwolf, Weights & Biases
items.excerpt: An agent repairs a broken git repository and earns a perfect score, but the run stays out of the default leaderboard because it tested only one task. Wolfram Ravenwolf uses that distinction to build an evaluation pipeline where every score can be traced back to its conditions. WolfBench compares the average, best and worst runs, the tasks solved at least once, and the tasks solved every time. Repeating the same configuration exposes the gap between a lucky success and dependable behavior. The configuration includes six layers: benchmark, runner, sandbox, agent, model service and settings. Versions, provider routing, system prompts, resource limits and timeouts all affect what the result actually measures. The live workflow launches a Terminal Bench task through Harbor, collects the results, filters incomplete runs in a Marimo dashboard, and turns valid runs into an interactive leaderboard. Weave preserves the trajectories behind the bars so reviewers can inspect commands, messages and failures. Ravenwolf examines two traps in interpreting the results: a cheaper model can consume enough tokens to raise total cost, and greater reasoning effort can lower the score when it leaves too little time to execute commands. Infrastructure failures need different treatment from genuine task failures, while zero temperature still does not guarantee identical runs. The resulting comparison helps teams choose a configuration for their own constraints, with costs and consistency visible alongside the headline score. items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: How Secrets Leak Through AI Agents (and How to Stop It) — Venice AI
items.excerpt: A private model doesn't make a private product. The leaks happen in everything you build around it. Joshua Mo, lead developer relations engineer at Venice AI and previously lead maintainer of the Rust AI framework Rig, explains why privacy matters (one breach and users leave, and less stored data means a smaller blast radius) and how Venice approaches it: no stored prompts, anonymized requests to closed providers, models in trusted execution environments, and split-key encrypted storage. Then he shows where agent systems leak: logs that quietly capture prompts and secrets, and secrets fetched from a vault straight into the reasoning layer, where a tool call can exfiltrate them. His patterns: hashed IDs instead of personal data, split-key custody, revocable handles, narrow agent scope, a classifier in front of the agent to catch prompt injection, wiring the vault to the execution layer instead of the LLM, sandboxes plus permission monitoring, and confidential compute with verifiable attestations. He closes on the open problem of confidential tool calls. items.title: Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA
items.excerpt: 50,000 seed examples become 7,000 training records after generation and filtering. Dhruv Nathawani uses that funnel to explain how NVIDIA builds synthetic data that teaches a model to search, rather than answer from memory. The starting material is a set of walks through Wikidata: connected entities become riddles whose answers require multiple searches. Data Designer turns those seeds into questions, tool calls and responses, with Tavily providing search through MCP. The goal is a reusable pipeline for teaching a chosen behavior, with search serving as the worked example. Three notebooks build the workflow in stages. The first combines seed topics, difficulty samplers, prompt templates, structured outputs and model judges to generate question and answer pairs. The second adds tool access and captures search traces. The third creates search riddles from graph paths and produces complete trajectories for supervised finetuning. Previewing a few records before running a batch makes the process inspectable and easier to revise. Nathawani then examines the difficult part: verifying that generated answers are correct when even the source graph can become stale. Model judgments, deterministic checks and human review contribute different evidence; no single score establishes dataset quality. Questions distinguish seed generation from agent execution, explore reinforcement learning alternatives and discuss other training tasks. The closing examples use synthetic personas to preserve demographic distributions, while the broader lesson remains practical: design for diversity, inspect examples, overproduce, filter and version the recipe. items.excerpt: A small refund feature passes through planning, implementation, local checks and pull request review before it is considered complete. Nnenna Ndukwe uses SignalPay, a deliberately narrow FastAPI payments application, to turn that sequence into quality gates for an AI coding agent. Participants choose a refund or capture retry workflow, identify the relevant payment rules and create both an implementation plan and a build execution plan. The point is to give the agent an explicit definition of the expected behavior, constraints, verification commands and evidence it must produce. Ndukwe installs repository skills, connects Qodo and walks through the planning templates in Codex. The templates carry assumptions, risk, skill routing, acceptance criteria and the state of the current branch into implementation. After the agent opens a pull request, Qodo adds review findings informed by the codebase and organizational rules. The workshop shows how to inspect those findings, document fixes or deferrals and use a resolver skill to address the feedback and rerun verification. Audience questions test the boundaries: how rules are inferred and approved, how severity controls merge blocking, when verification should run again and how local checks relate to cloud review. The exercise finishes by resolving the remaining issues rather than treating a passing local run as the end of the workflow. Its reusable artifact is a structured process that keeps plans, code changes and review evidence connected. The budget example becomes an evaluation that checks whether returned prices actually satisfy the requested range. Agent experiments replay failure datasets against a deployed development endpoint and compare quality, latency and cost before a change ships. Setup pauses and live questions cover keys, tracing and the skills installation. The closing workflow connects automatic detection and repair to validation on real failures, with a reviewable proposal for a human to assess. items.title: Can Your Agent Hear You Now? Building Live Voice Agents with Gemini — Thor Schaeff
items.excerpt: An agent that hears you, sees you, and answers in your language, in real time. Here's how to build one with Gemini. Thor Schaeff, who works on developer experience at Google DeepMind, runs a set of live demos of Gemini's real-time and media models. He builds an illustrated story with Gemini Live and a fast Nano Banana image model, using the stateful Interactions API to keep characters and style consistent between images. He has the audience scan a QR code to hear the talk in their own language with Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, then calls up an AI radio DJ that uses Lyria 3 to generate a reggaeton track on request. He explains how the Live API works: a stateful WebSocket session that takes in text, audio and video and streams back audio plus a transcript, using a native audio model rather than a speech-to-text and text-to-speech pipeline. It supports 90 languages, interruptions, tool calls and Google Search grounding. He ends with a voice and vision demo in Google AI Studio. items.excerpt: A customer service agent looks up an account, checks an order, and handles a refund. The harder part is controlling what happens between those steps and keeping that control when the agent reaches production. Elizabeth Fuentes Leone and Sandhya Subramani build the workflow with Strands Agents, starting with a system prompt and three tools backed by mock customer data. They inspect messages and tool calls, add a conversational interface, then introduce a hook that limits tool invocations. Lowering the limit makes the constraint visible in a live test. An audience question separates blocking another tool call from ending the agent's turn, showing why a control needs a precise definition. The next modules add skills and steering. Markdown instructions provide account troubleshooting, order tracking, and refund procedures when they are needed, while steering handlers check workflow order and response tone. The presenters compare programmatic checks with instructions left to a probabilistic model, then move the same customer service code into Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The deployment walkthrough covers the application entry point, local testing, runtime setup, generated infrastructure, and a successful invocation. It also shows the observability configuration needed to inspect sessions, traces, and token use. The result is a path from a small notebook agent to a deployed service, with explicit places to add context, enforce constraints, and examine behavior. items.title: RAG Needs a Map: Using GraphRAG to Retrieve Connected Context — Nyah Macklin, Neo4j
items.excerpt: An agent answering questions about a course needs more than the five chunks closest to a query. It also needs the connections between lessons, concepts, and the sources behind its answer. Nyah Macklin builds that retrieval path with Neo4j, combining vector search with a knowledge graph that people can inspect and query. The workshop starts with the difference between semantic similarity and relationships, then walks through GraphAcademy, an Aura database, and a Python environment. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from course material, embeddings support similarity search, and Cypher exposes the resulting structure. Vectors remain part of the system; the graph adds connected context and a way to answer questions that require traversal or aggregation. The hands on build moves from a knowledge graph pipeline to an agent in Aura. Macklin creates a vector index, configures a lesson search tool, adds a retrieval query that returns related graph data, and enables natural language questions through text to Cypher. The agent answers a question about temperature using course content and displays its sources. A lesson count prompts a closer check of the underlying database query, showing why visible evidence matters even after the pipeline works. The final code walkthrough covers chunking, entity types, relationship types, and a schema that guides extraction rather than leaving the model to invent the graph's structure. items.title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
items.excerpt: Ask a vector store for the PRs you merged last week and it can hand back one that is semantically perfect and three years old. Peter Werry builds context engines at Unblocked, and his thesis is that RAG, meaning similarity search, is only half of retrieval. Engineering context lives in pull requests, review comments, tickets, wikis, and chat, and all of it has structure: authors, dates, states, labels, relationships. Dumping it all in a vector store and reranking fails any question with a temporal or structural half. So the other half is turning natural language into a real database query, where the model does not answer the question, it writes the query. The workshop walks six stacked pull requests that turn a stubbed query playground into a working engine over a GitHub repository. Four pieces make the query reliable. Schema discovery samples three hundred documents and merges them into one tree, with procedural code rather than a model inferring types and enums. Identity resolution maps Peter to his GitHub login with simple fuzzy matching. Query planning passes the schema, forces a name extraction tool call, and includes the current date. Validation is deny by default: an allow list of operators keeps a function clause from running JavaScript on the server, and hidden metadata fields are wiped and reinjected for tenant isolation. A retry loop feeds validation and execution errors back to the model, which exposes the need for full text search when exact match fails. The same engine then powers a chat agent, and the Q&A covers scaling schemas with summaries, continuous ingestion, why Slack holds the why questions, MCP, and hybrid search. items.title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
items.excerpt: Your voice agent's dashboard says it's fast. Your callers say it feels robotic. They're both right. Jesse Hall, staff developer advocate at LiveKit, explains how to build voice agents that feel human. He shows why leaderboards can't pick your models (scores measure one model, but you ship a pipeline, and errors compound from speech-to-text to the LLM to text-to-speech) and why measured latency isn't what your callers hear. He covers buying time like a person does while tools run, plays a hotel-receptionist demo that handles interruptions and a caller changing his mind, explains LiveKit's audio-based turn detection (4.5% of users cut off vs 9.9% for the best alternative), and lays out the window that matters: a second and a half end to end still works, and around 600 milliseconds starts to feel human. He ends with LiveKit's open-source benchmark you can run against your own agent, a sneak peek of a voice-tuned Gemma model on LiveKit Inference, and a checklist. items.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
items.excerpt: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run. Tags: version-control

items.text: If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more. The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive. Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on. As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have. You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

items.title: An AI Future Without the Lock-In — Remy Guercio, Tailscale
items.excerpt: The era of unlimited AI budgets is over, and most teams are locked into whichever tools they picked first. Remy Guercio, who works on Tailscale's AI gateway Aperture, looks back at a year of AI lock-in and asks how teams get out of it while proving real ROI. He breaks an internal AI deployment into four layers (the models, the data connectors like MCP, CLIs and APIs, the interface, and the sandbox) and argues an AI gateway is what keeps them swappable. He shows how Aperture uses your Tailscale network for identity instead of shared API keys, sets budgets per model (unlimited for cheap models, tight for frontier ones), works as both an LLM and MCP gateway, handles authentication for Cursor, Claude Code and Codex in one place, and keeps logs you can use to diagnose what an agent did. In this talk: • Why unlimited AI budgets are ending, and what ROI maxing means • The four layers of an AI stack and where lock-in hides • How an AI gateway ties identity, budgets and logs together • Aperture as both an LLM and MCP gateway SPEAKER Remy Guercio, Strategic Projects, Tailscale X: https://twitter.com/remyguercio GitHub: https://github.com/remyguercio LINKS Aperture docs: https://tailscale.com/docs/aperture Aperture: https://aperture.tailscale.com Tailscale: https://tailscale.com CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:45 A year of AI lock-in 2:05 The end of unlimited budgets 2:45 Wasted tokens 3:20 How do we get out? 4:44 Finance wants answers 5:14 ROI maxing 6:09 The four layers 8:09 Meet Aperture 9:24 How most AI gateways work 10:09 Identity from the tailnet 10:44 Built with tsnet 12:04 Budgets per model 12:44 LLM and MCP gateway 14:04 Auth in one place 16:49 Sandboxes 18:04 Why you need a gateway Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. items.title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
items.excerpt: Most models learn text first and get vision bolted on later. MiniMax M3 learned both from the very first training step. Olive, who works on reinforcement learning research at MiniMax, goes inside MiniMax M3, an open-weight model with frontier-level coding and agentic ability, a 1 million token context window and native multimodality. She explains MSA, MiniMax's sparse attention design (about 9x faster prefill and 15x faster decoding than full attention): an index branch that picks which blocks matter and a sparse branch that attends only to those, and why existing designs like DeepSeek's DSA didn't fit grouped-query attention or GPU memory access. Then she covers training with text and vision from step zero, why adding vision later gave unstable results, what the attention maps show, and why 3D attention inside the vision transformer improves visual understanding. In this talk: • What makes MiniMax M3 different: agentic coding, 1M context, native multimodal • How MSA sparse attention works, and why DSA didn't fit • Block-level retrieval and kernels built for real GPUs • Why training on text and vision from step zero beats adding vision later SPEAKER Olive Song, RL Lead, MiniMax X: https://x.com/olive_jy_song LINKS MiniMax: https://www.minimax.io MiniMax M3 (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 (Hugging Face): https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 tech report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13392 MSA (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MSA CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:03 Meet MiniMax M3 1:37 1M token context 2:57 Sparse attention: index and sparse branches 4:17 Why not DeepSeek's DSA? 5:07 Problems with existing sparse attention 5:37 GPU memory access 7:01 MSA: what we changed 7:46 Block-level retrieval 8:21 Efficient kernels 9:01 Multi…

items.text: Ignoring the actors in the latest debacle of VC, “philosophically” you can’t have both.. > ask a fund to show conviction, and ask to double down especially when the chips are down. > ask them not do contracted pro rata just because it’s convenient to you from a dilution perspective or the lead fund that’s trying to get their ownership targets. For founders, another reminder to choose your partners AND contracts well. It’s so so so important. Get a good independent lawyer who will spell this out for you. items.title: AI Agents Don't Read Your Policy Docs. They Hit Your APIs — Gravitee
items.excerpt: You can write all the rules you want in a markdown file. Your agent can still call the API. Sam, CTO at Gravity, skips the slides and runs five live scenarios against a hotel-booking agent to show why governance belongs in the infrastructure, not in the agent's instructions. Running on the Gravity Gateway with a Databricks backend, Sonnet and Groq, he shows the gateway blocking a destructive "delete all bookings" tool call, stopping an attempt to pull every guest's personal data, rate-limiting a buggy agent that fires the same request eight times, serving repeated questions from a semantic cache, and rejecting an oversized prompt before it ever reaches the LLM. He also covers telemetry across your agents, decoupling from any one hyperscaler, trimming bloated MCP tool lists, and shadow AI on employee laptops. In this talk: • Why prompts and policy docs can't enforce what agents do • Blocking destructive tool calls and data exfiltration at the gateway • Rate limits, semantic caching and token limits that cut cost • Observability, decoupling from vendors, and trimming MCP tools SPEAKER Sam, CTO, Gravity CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 Agents without governance 1:32 Move policy to the gateway 2:57 Demo 1: Blocking destructive tools 4:57 Demo 2: Stopping data exfiltration 6:56 Demo 3: Runaway repeat requests 8:21 Demo 4: Semantic caching 11:01 Demo 5: Blocking oversized prompts 12:21 Expensive agent habits 15:01 Avoiding vendor lock-in 15:41 Trimming MCP tools 16:16 Shadow AI 16:56 Wrap-up Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. items.title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
items.excerpt: Vector search can't answer "which PRs did I merge last week?" A relational context engine can, and it cuts token burn along the way. Peter Werry, founding engineer at Unblocked, explains what a context engine is and why coding agents need more than code search: the PRs, Slack threads and incident history that explain why the code is the way it is. He shows Claude sessions with and without that context, including one with about a 50% drop in cost and one that traced a regression to a model switch. Then he builds Unblocked's open-source document query engine step by step: automatic schema discovery, identity resolution across systems, query validation that blocks dangerous operators, retries that feed errors back to the model, and full-text search. He closes with the open-source context engine simulator for testing whether pre-gathered context helps your agents. In this talk: • What a context engine is, and how it lowers cost on real agent sessions • Why vector stores can't answer structural questions about your work • Turning plain-English questions into safe, validated database queries • Schema discovery, identity resolution, retries and full-text search SPEAKER Peter Werry, Founding Engineer, Unblocked LINKS Unblocked: https://getunblocked.com Document query engine (GitHub): https://github.com/unblocked/document-query-engine Unblocked on X: https://x.com/get_unblocked CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 Agenda 2:22 Demo: agents with and without context 4:17 Half the cost 4:57 Tracing a model regression 6:17 Let's build 7:11 Questions vector search can't answer 8:21 The hard part: scaffolding 9:46 The document query engine 10:31 Automatic schema discovery 12:26 Identity resolution 13:45 Validating queries 15:50 Retries 16:35 Full-text search 18:30 Context engine simulator Recorde…

items.text: Agent capabilities will soon evolve at RSI pace. Agentic security (identity, permissions, observability) will need to outpace this. The evolutionary direction of the broader agents space is capability -> trust -> autonomy The first phase has been about capability - can the combination of model + harness + tools + context reliably get work done? Capabilities have gotten pretty far, so the focus now shifts to trust…does the harness / system take the right action with right permissions? Can we observe it, audit it and establish accountability? A lot of serious work has already gone into these problems over the last couple of years. Now the challenge gets more important. and harder.

items.title: Zero Cold Starts: Serverless AI Agents on Akamai Functions — Thorsten Hans
items.excerpt: Cold starts, proprietary SDKs and one-region deployments slow AI apps down. WebAssembly at the edge removes all three. Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate at Akamai, shows how to build and ship MCP servers and AI agents with Spin, the open-source WebAssembly framework, and run them on Akamai Functions, a globally distributed serverless platform with no cold starts. He explains why WebAssembly on the server is fast, portable and sandboxed by default, then live-codes MCP servers with wasmcp: scaffolding tools in TypeScript and Rust, composing them into a full server, testing with MCP Inspector, deploying it worldwide in about 60 seconds with one command, and calling its tools from the Zed editor. He finishes with an agent built on the Vercel AI SDK, backed by a model on a Linode GPU, and explains how memory snapshots keep apps warm. items.text: Good post to start thinking through the long term safety approaches to managing intelligence in an enterprise. As agents begin to do vastly more task execution in the organization than humans, our need to secure, govern, control, and audit that work will become paramount. You’ll have agents operating against most of your most valuable data; they’ll be making decisions that will be harder and harder to reverse engineer; we’ll need to understand the liability and accountability regimes when models make decisions for us; and we need ways of containing the blast radius of accidentally or intentionally malicious agents. “Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system. Not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised, and the architecture of containment and control must account for that” In a sense, AI will need to have its “zero trust” era that security saw. And all of this leads to needing various layers of protection and auditability of what agents are doing, what data they can work with, and controls for when things go wrong. And a huge opportunity right now for those building such systems across the enterprise.

items.title: The Lethal Trifecta Is Already on Your Laptops — Michael Patterson, Coder
items.excerpt: Your coding agent can read private data, take in untrusted content and talk to the internet. That's the lethal trifecta, and it's already running on your developers' laptops. Michael Patterson, staff solutions engineer at Coder, explains Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally) and why agents like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw running on a laptop hit all three. He covers prompt injection, what blocks big companies from rolling out agents (CISO concerns, shadow AI on personal subscriptions, alert fatigue, skeptical senior engineers), and three architectural guardrails: cloud development environments that isolate the agent, a model proxy that logs traffic and strips sensitive data before it reaches the LLM provider, and an agent firewall that denies commands and domains you didn't allow. items.text: Agents spawning other agents, agents operating in the background on every task, and agent swarms will consume 1,000X more tokens than people prompting agents 1 at a time. The usage of AI as a chat system that can only work for you at the pace that you can prompt it will seem like a relic within a year or two. The vast, vast majority of tokens will be consumed by agents that are just doing continuous work for us in the background and in our workflows. This is why we’re still so early in the curve of AI agent adoption right now, and how much more compute and infrastructure build out will be needed to sustain this.

items.title: From 15% to 90% GPU Utilization: Fix the Data Pipeline, Not the Model
items.excerpt: Your GPUs might be waiting on your data, not your model. This pipeline went from 15% to 90% GPU utilization. Tarun Sunkaraneni from Amazon AGI shows that the hardest part of fast multimodal training often isn't the GPU at all, but keeping it fed with data. Training a Qwen3-VL-style model on images stored in S3, the baseline pipeline spent about 85% of its time waiting on data, mostly loading, decoding and resizing images one at a time. He fixes the bottlenecks one by one: concurrency with asyncio and Ray actors, prefetching so data is ready before the trainer asks, and Ray's object store to stop copying big image tensors between processes. Then, at production scale, a new bottleneck appears on a single machine's network card, solved by spreading workers across nodes and using zero-copy reads, which gave another 50% throughput. In this talk: • Why multimodal training is often CPU- and IO-bound, not GPU-bound • Concurrency, prefetching and zero-copy transfer with Ray • Choosing between asyncio, threads and processes around the GIL • Why some settings only pay off at scale SPEAKER Tarun Sunkaraneni, Amazon AGI GitHub: https://github.com/TSunny007 Website: https://tsunny007.github.io/ LINKS Ray: https://www.ray.io CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:45 Is training really GPU-bound? 1:10 Four bottlenecks 1:50 Why multimodal is CPU-heavy 2:45 The wait-time ratio 3:35 Our stack 4:10 The data 4:35 System layout 5:15 Baseline: 15% utilization 6:20 Fix 1: concurrency 7:05 Async, threads or processes? 8:10 Asyncio plus Ray actors 9:15 Fix 2: prefetching 10:40 Fix 3: zero-copy with Ray's object store 12:20 Recap: 85% to 20% wait time 12:55 Scaling up: a new bottleneck 13:25 The network card bottleneck 14:35 Spread scheduling and zero copy 15:35 Lessons Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2…

items.title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
items.excerpt: A 4 billion parameter model, trained with RL for under $500, beat its 235 billion parameter sibling on real financial questions. Charles Dickens, research scientist at Snorkel AI, shares how Snorkel and UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab trained a small model to beat a much bigger one. Working from SEC 10-K filings, they built FinQA, a financial question-answering dataset with expert-validated answers, and found even frontier models hallucinating table schemas, flooding their own context, and repeating failed strategies. Using the open-source rLLM framework and reinforcement learning with a simple pass/fail reward, they trained a Qwen3 4B model for under $500 that reached about 60% versus 51% for the 235B model. The skills transferred to harder multi-table questions without hurting general tool use. Surprisingly, simpler training data and simpler rewards worked best, because the real bottleneck was disciplined tool use, not reasoning depth. In this talk: • How the FinQA dataset was built and verified from 10-K filings • Failure modes: hallucinated schemas, context flooding, poor recovery • Training a 4B model with RL in rLLM for under $500 • Why simple data and binary rewards beat fancier setups SPEAKER Charles Dickens, Senior Applied Research Scientist, Snorkel AI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/charles-dickens/ GitHub: https://github.com/dickensc LINKS Snorkel blog: how a 4B model outsmarted a 235B giant: https://snorkel.ai/blog/how-tool-discipline-let-a-4b-model-outsmart-a-235b-giant-on-financial-tasks/ rLLM-FinQA-4B on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/rLLM/rLLM-FinQA-4B rLLM framework: https://github.com/rllm-org/rllm Snorkel Open Benchmarks Grants: https://benchmarks.snorkel.ai/ Snorkel AI: https://snorkel.ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 Specialization can beat…

items.title: Why Your Company Needs a Context Graph (and How to Build It) — Gil Feig, Merge
items.excerpt: Your agent can tell you why one customer was upset. Ask which customers were upset last year, and it falls apart. Gil Feig, co-founder and CTO of Merge, explains why every company needs a context graph, a company brain that brings together third-party data, structured context, memories and skills. Using the question "which customers were upset last week?", he shows why connecting a few MCP servers isn't enough: live API lookups can't search across large datasets, so you need a synced copy for semantic queries, alongside live calls for simple lookups. He walks through the architecture: a router, synced and live context, a summarizer, and skills and memory that encode how your company actually defines things like a happy customer. He covers four tiers of context including derived summaries, a decision flowchart for when to use cache or live data, and why every answer must keep track of where its data came from. In this talk: • Why MCP live lookups can't answer questions across large datasets • Combining synced data, live lookups, a router and a summarizer • Why company skills and memory belong in the context layer • Traceability: where data came from, when, and what invalidates it SPEAKER Gil Feig, Co-founder & CTO, Merge LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/gilfeig/ X: https://x.com/gilfeig LINKS Merge: https://www.merge.dev Merge Agent Handler: https://www.merge.dev/merge-agent-handler Merge Gateway: https://www.merge.dev/gateway Merge on X: https://x.com/merge_api CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:02 About Merge 2:17 What is a context graph? 2:27 The company brain 3:17 Example: why was a customer upset? 4:02 Why live lookups break 4:22 MCP alone isn't enough 5:07 Sync a copy of the data 6:17 The router and summarizer 6:47 Why skills and memory belong 7:57 No magic, just physics…

items.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
items.excerpt: Deno is joining Cloudflare The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog .) The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year: We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News: It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or netw…

items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Review Is Expensive: How to Stop Shipping AI Slop — Gabriel Martinez, G2i
items.excerpt: Slop isn't AI-written code. It's work that looks finished before the thinking is. Gabriel "Gabo" Martinez, engineering manager and self-described slop warden at G2i, explains what slop really is: what happens when generation outruns judgment, when ambiguity gets cleared with guesses and nobody notices there was a choice to make. He's not anti-AI, but argues we need to sober up. Code is still a liability, agents make a messy codebase messier faster, and quick prototypes convince stakeholders the hard part is done. He covers the pressure to merge faster than you can review, thousand-line PRs, 20-page AI docs that push the thinking onto reviewers, and why generation is cheap but evaluation is expensive. His fixes are conventions, diagrams as the review surface, small reviewable changes and clear ownership, inspired by Rails, plus why G2i built ORC. In this talk: • What slop is, and why it's about missing judgment, not AI • Why code is a liability and AI makes the ball of mud bigger • Incentives that push teams to merge faster than they can review • Conventions, diagrams and small changes that keep humans in control SPEAKER Gabriel Martinez, Engineering Manager, G2i LINKS ORC by G2i: https://orc.ai G2i: https://www.g2i.ai G2i on X: https://x.com/g2i_ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 What slop is 1:12 The real danger: choices nobody saw 1:52 Time to sober up 2:27 What agents can't replace 2:51 How we got here 3:06 Code is a liability 4:01 A bigger ball of mud 4:11 Lines spent, not produced 5:01 Accountability 5:31 The prototype illusion 6:50 "It's not free" 7:25 Pressure to merge faster 7:45 Performance anxiety 8:45 Thousand-line PRs 9:30 The 20-page doc problem 10:14 Generation is cheap, review isn't 10:29 Twitter hype and the Ralph loop 11:39 Why code shape still matters 12:34…

items.title: From Context to Memory: Your Agents Need a Real Memory Layer — Anders Swanson, Oracle
items.excerpt: Your agent rereads the same files every session because nothing it learned was saved. Anders Swanson, developer evangelist for Oracle Database, treats agent memory as a systems problem. Context windows aren't memory, bigger windows aren't the fix, and markdown scratch pads and grep don't scale. Keep going down that road and you'll end up building your own database. He walks through the pattern modern memory systems are converging on: formation, recall, evolution and evaluation, plus governance. That means typed memories (episodic, semantic, procedural and working state), a storage schema with vectors, text indexes, graph links, time and audit history, redaction before anything is written, and hybrid search that blends several retrieval methods. He covers failure modes like stale, mis-scoped, poisoned and conflicting memories, and why feedback is what closes the loop. items.title: Designing CLIs for Agents, Not Humans — Pedro Lopez, Airbyte
items.excerpt: Airbyte built both an MCP server and a CLI so agents can use its data. Here's what each one is actually good for. Pedro Lopez, software engineer at Airbyte, shares lessons from building two ways for AI agents to reach company data through Airbyte's Context Store, a search-optimized index of tools like Zendesk, Stripe and HubSpot. Both are thin interfaces over one platform, built from OpenAPI specs. For the MCP server, he explains why to keep the tool count small and use progressive discovery, why OAuth is the only realistic way to sign in, why users expect long-lived sessions, and why URL elicitation isn't ready across clients yet. For the CLI, he explains designing for agents instead of humans: JSON in and JSON out, consistent noun-verb commands, skills that ship with the tool, and no interactive prompts. He closes with when to choose MCP and when to choose a CLI. items.title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
items.excerpt: You correct your agent. It says "You're absolutely right." Five minutes later, after compaction, it makes the same mistake again. Greg Pstrucha, who works on the infrastructure behind Seer, Sentry's debugging agent, argues you should stop re-prompting your coding agent and start codifying the rules you keep repeating. Agents have no memory, so the same elementary mistakes come back: overly defensive code, useless tests, endpoints nobody needs. Tests, strict types and especially linters turn those corrections into deterministic checks, and with agents, writing a custom lint rule is now cheap. He shows real examples from Sentry: lint rules that keep endpoints in sync with the OpenAPI schema, and a long game of whack-a-mole to keep agent skills accurate. For qualitative judgment, he uses written policies and a "Grumpy Engineer" review loop, and warns that agents will game any number you hand them, like test coverage. In this talk: • Why re-prompting fails, and why lint rules are now cheap to write • Mining your transcripts and PR reviews for rules worth enforcing • Examples from Sentry: API schema checks and linting agent skills • Policies and review agents for what linters can't catch, and why metrics get gamed SPEAKER Greg Pstrucha, Staff Software Engineer, Sentry LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/greg-pstrucha/ LINKS Sentry Seer: https://sentry.io/product/seer/ Sentry: https://sentry.io Sentry on X: https://x.com/sentry CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:38 Who still reads AI code? 1:13 The code is bad 1:58 "You're absolutely right" 2:23 Stop prompting, start codifying 2:58 Tests, strict types, linters 4:08 Why lint rules are cheap now 5:28 Mine your transcripts for rules 5:58 Custom lint rules 6:43 Example: keeping APIs in sync 7:52 Example: linting agent skills 9:17 Whack-a-m…

items.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
items.excerpt: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want…

items.text: This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy. Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models. The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data. Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

items.text: Met a close friend who’s also a seed stage founder today.. They have been growing but runway is dwindling and he wanted advice on what he should do next. Stellar customers, getting close to a $1M in revenue. Not a rocket ship, but not bad at all. He thinks he’s a bit early since the models haven’t caught up to the capabilities he wants but he also really feels the opportunity cost. I have this same exact conversation at least 2x a week. In this moment, you only have essentially three options: 1) if you have intense belief in the company, be a cockroach and get to default profitable. once the capabilities get there, you feel the demand, then go raise a large round and go for the jugular. 2) find an orthogonal area that is much more relevant and growing like crazy. ride the coat tails of new existing capabilities and push hard to capture them quickly using unfair advantages. and if you don’t have that, then.. 3) sell / get acquihired and join a far more ambitious company that has figured out a lot of the things you haven’t. And then get back to starting a new company 1-2 years later when you find the next thing you want to build. It’s hard but honestly those are the three options you have. And it really depends what category you’re in. The bar continues to get harder every month on how to cross the chasm from seed -> series A. The old school metrics are just not relevant anymore and in this consensus market there’s only a few categories where there’s tremendous pull on the VC front. You could lament that this is the state of the market, but it’s better to know it’s happening than be oblivious on what is actually happening. I get to share this directly which makes me uncomfortable but at least someone has to say it out loud 🙈

items.title: AI Writes More PRs. Who Validates Them? — Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Sonar
items.excerpt: AI means more PRs, bigger PRs, and more bugs. Your choice is to slow down or rubber-stamp, unless validation gets automated too. Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, co-founder of Gitar (now part of Sonar), focuses on verifying code. CI and code review are where quality gates live, and they get slower and more expensive as teams grow. AI makes it worse with more and bigger PRs, leaving teams to either slow down or rubber-stamp and risk incidents. His answer is agentic validation: an agent that reviews PRs with as little noise as possible, explains CI failures and catches flaky tests, fixes issues until the PR is green, and approves and merges based on rules you set. He describes how users build trust step by step toward full automation, the insights it gives platform teams and leaders, what's under the hood (control plane, custom harness and LLM proxy), and why combining agents with program analysis in SonarQube beats either alone. In this talk: • Why AI-generated code turns CI and code review into a bottleneck • Agentic validation: review, CI analysis, autofix and auto-merge • How teams build trust step by step toward fully automated PRs • Why agents plus program analysis beat either alone SPEAKER Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Co-founder, Gitar (now part of Sonar) LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aliadl/ X: https://x.com/aadltaba LINKS Gitar by Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com/products/gitar/ Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com Sonar on X: https://x.com/SonarSource CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:43 CI and code review: the critical path 1:57 Failures cost hours and days 2:57 AI makes it worse 3:22 Slow down or rubber-stamp 3:42 Agentic validation 4:07 Noise-free code review 4:42 CI failures and flaky tests 5:02 Autofix until green 5:27 Auto-approve and auto-merge 5:47 The path to full autom…

items.title: ttok 1.0
items.excerpt: Release: ttok 1.0 I released ttok 0.4 , ran uv tool upgrade ttok , piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead! I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0. OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same: All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus. Tags: projects , ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , tokenization

items.title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
items.excerpt: Your agent scores great on benchmarks. Then real customers use it and it breaks. Felipe Blanes from the Amazon AGI Lab shares what he learned working directly with customers of Nova Act, Amazon's service for building browser agents, from research preview to general availability on AWS. He calls the core problem the benchmark illusion: static evals look great until customers do things nobody expected, and then all you have left is hope. His fix is an eval flywheel built around the customer: define success the way the customer does, capture signals (including by talking to customers), diagnose gaps in the model, harness or product, and feed them into decisions. He explains the trust cliff (80% reliability feels like more work; around 92% feels trustworthy), why being open about limits builds more trust than higher benchmarks, surprising use cases from Amazon Leo, Hertz and Sola, and four principles for keeping evals fresh. items.title: How a Remote Company Builds AI Fluency — Em Shreve, Automattic
items.excerpt: Handing people AI tools doesn't change how they work. Giving them real time to learn does. Em Shreve, head of AI enablement at Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com and Tumblr with over 1,400 people in 82 countries, explains how a fully remote company builds AI fluency. Their bet: people need real time to learn, not just tools. So they run two-week, in-person programs that are half workshops and half real project work, for engineers, cross-functional teams and non-technical groups like finance and leadership. She covers the curriculum (skills, MCPs, hooks, autonomous agents) and why it has to change constantly, their internal MCP server, and how every graduate becomes a multiplier through guides, local meetups, AI ride-alongs and an always-on help channel. She shares what they measure, and projects people built in two weeks, including a tool built by a support teammate rather than an engineer. In this talk: • Why AI enablement needs dedicated time, not just tool access • A two-week program: half workshops, half real project work • Turning every graduate into a multiplier across a remote company • What to measure, and what people built in two weeks SPEAKER Em Shreve, Head of AI Enablement, Automattic Website: https://emdash.codes GitHub: https://github.com/emdashcodes LINKS Automattic: https://automattic.com Automattic on X: https://x.com/automattic CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:55 Our bet: real time to learn 1:15 Two-week in-person programs 1:30 Half workshops, half real projects 2:40 Engineers, cross-functional and non-technical 3:25 The engineering curriculum 4:49 Keeping the curriculum current 5:24 An internal MCP server 6:19 Every graduate is a multiplier 6:29 7 cohorts and counting 7:09 Guides and local meetups 8:09 AI ride-alongs 8:44 Shared skills and MCPs 9:04 A…

items.title: Brains vs Hands: How to Run AI Agents Safely in Production — Viren Baraiya
items.excerpt: Let the model decide what should happen next. Never let it improvise how a production cluster gets restarted. Viren Baraiya, co-founder and CTO of Orkes and the original creator of Netflix Conductor, explains how to run agents in production. Real agents aren't just chatbots: they run on schedules, react to events, coordinate other agents and can run for months, so the harness around them starts to look like an application, much like a set of microservices. His key idea is a clean split between the brain and the hands. The LLM plans what should happen next; a deterministic, durable harness does the actual work, with approval gates, idempotent steps and recorded side effects. He frames agent harnesses as late-bound sagas, workflows the agent assembles at runtime, and demos an SRE agent whose plan is compiled into a Conductor workflow, executed, checked and re-planned over two loops. In this talk: • Background, scheduled, event-driven and long-running agents • Why the harness is the application, mixing deterministic and non-deterministic parts • The brain and the hands: the LLM plans, the harness executes • Demo: an SRE agent's plan compiled into a durable workflow SPEAKER Viren Baraiya, Co-founder & CTO, Orkes X: https://x.com/virenbaraiya LINKS Orkes: https://orkes.io Orkes on X: https://x.com/orkesio CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:47 Who runs agents in production? 1:12 Beyond the hello-world agent 1:52 Background, scheduled and event-driven agents 2:27 Coordinators and multi-agent systems 3:02 Agents are applications, not components 3:12 Lessons from microservices 4:22 The harness is the application 5:02 Deterministic and non-deterministic parts 6:02 Harnesses run for seconds or months 6:41 Durability is table stakes 7:26 How the loop works 8:21 The agent plans, the harness exe…

items.title: We Mapped 115 Microservices for Our Coding Agents — Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Postman
items.excerpt: Coding agents are great inside one repo. Postman has 115 microservices and thousands of endpoints. Kamalakannan Nandagopal, staff engineer at Postman, shares how Postman made coding agents work across a real distributed system. Docs go stale, skills and MCPs are only as good as their context, and agent memory stays stuck with one person. Borrowing from Postman's go-to-market team, they realized APIs are the context layer, and built an API context graph that maps every service, endpoint, implementation and call, all the way down to databases, with every data point grounded in code or production telemetry. He shares evals built from real PRs and design decisions: big wins on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment, an honest failure when the graph went stale, the finding that 75% of PRs touched APIs, and a 21-page architecture review the agent produced on its own. In this talk: • Why coding agents struggle with distributed systems and microservices • Building an API context graph grounded in code and telemetry • Eval results on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment • Why keeping the graph fresh matters as much as building it SPEAKER Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Staff Engineer, Postman LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/kamalakannan-nandagopal-3650818a/ LINKS Postman Context Graph API: https://blog.postman.com/introducing-the-context-graph-api-one-map-of-your-api-ecosystem/ Context Graph docs: https://learning.postman.com/docs/use/context-graph/get-started Postman: https://www.postman.com Postman on X: https://x.com/getpostman CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 115 microservices 1:02 From autocomplete to autonomous agents 1:42 Real systems are distributed 2:12 Docs go stale 2:36 Skills, MCPs and agent memory 3:21 What the go-to-market team learned 4:01 APIs are the con…
