items.title: Turning Agent Memory Into Skills That Work — Will Lyon, Neo4j
items.excerpt: Agents finish a task, then forget what they learned. Retrieval alone won't fix that. Will Lyon, senior product manager at Neo4j, explains why agent memory built on embeddings and retrieval isn't enough: recall isn't actionable knowledge. Agents need knowledge that is connected, typed and traceable. He shows Neo4j's model of agent memory as a context graph with short-term, long-term and reasoning memory, covering entity extraction and resolution, shared ontologies, and decision traces that let many agents learn from each other. Then he turns memory into action: distilling grounded, governed skills from the graph, based on Neo4j research that treats skills as typed execution graphs, with checks for grounding, coverage and coherence, and alerts when a skill goes stale. He demos the Neo4j Agent Memory Service distilling a patient-intake skill from a healthcare conversation. items.title: Your AI Agent Has No Nervous System — Matt Gibiec, Dynatrace
items.excerpt: Your coding agent is fast. But it can't see how your services actually run, so it guesses. Matt Gibiec, who leads AI-native solutions engineering at Dynatrace, explains why AI agents need something like a nervous system: real context from the environment they're changing. Agents get stuck in loops, cause operational and security issues, and are hard to measure, because they work fast but blind, only as good as the data they can see. He introduces Bluebox by Dynatrace, an observability agent for your coding agent, and walks through scenarios: bringing production dependencies into local testing so a change that works on your laptop doesn't break three other services, spotting issues before users feel them, suggesting fixes that account for the rest of the system, and briefing agents with real usage data before they build, with a human keeping final control. In this talk: • Why agents loop, hallucinate and break things without environment context • Bringing production dependencies into local testing • Catching problems early and tying them to the change that caused them • Planning before you prompt, with a human approving the final fix SPEAKER Matt Gibiec, Solutions Engineering, AI Native, Dynatrace LINKS Bluebox by Dynatrace: https://bluebox.ai Dynatrace: https://www.dynatrace.com Bluebox on X: https://x.com/Blueboxhq CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:35 About Dynatrace 1:00 What the title means 2:10 Stuck in a loop 2:50 Operations and security 3:30 How do you measure value? 4:34 Fast, but blind 6:34 Context is king 7:04 Introducing Bluebox 7:29 Works locally, breaks in production 9:09 Catch issues before users do 10:59 Fix without breaking other things 12:09 Plan before you prompt 13:29 A human stays in control 14:44 Try the preview Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in…

items.title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
items.excerpt: Reducto gave its whole team an MCP server with a tool for every endpoint. It broke the same day. Abhi Arya, who works on product at Reducto, argues that building agent-first software comes down to one question: who pays when the agent is wrong? He describes three approaches, auto mode, user-first, and agent experience in service of the user, and how Reducto learned the difference. A first MCP server with one tool per API endpoint demoed well but fell apart when the whole team used it: the agent built entire workflows confidently, and nobody could explain them. He deleted it in one commit and rebuilt with fewer tools that carry the structure of real work, plus a snapshot tool for live state. Then he made uncertainty visible, with confidence scores and an agent that asks instead of guessing, and added instrumentation that made the system improve on its own, until the sales team adopted it without being asked. In this talk: • Auto mode vs user-first vs agent experience in service of the user • Why one tool per API endpoint fails, and what to build instead • Making uncertainty visible: confidence scores and asking instead of guessing • Instrumentation that turns usage into a self-improving loop SPEAKER Abhi Arya, Product, Reducto LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/abhiaarya/ X: https://x.com/abhiarya GitHub: https://github.com/abhi-arya1 Website: https://abhi-arya1.github.io LINKS Reducto: https://reducto.ai Reducto MCP server docs: https://docs.reducto.ai/mcp-server Reducto on X: https://x.com/reductoai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:38 3 billion documents 1:48 What is agent-first software? 2:38 Who pays when the agent is wrong? 2:48 Auto mode, user-first, or in service of the user 3:57 Stuck in configuration 4:47 Version 1: a tool for every endpoint 5:27 It broke immediately 6…

items.subtitle: Madhu Guru · Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google -…
items.text: There are massive startup opportunities hiding in plain sight : every layer of the computing stack will need to be rebuilt for agents. For the last few years, most of the focus has been on making enterprise software agent-ready: APIs, connectors, MCPs. Now personal agents are forcing the same conversation for consumer products - e-commerce is an early example. This is just the tip of the iceberg. Now think about the rest of the stack: Desktop and mobile OSes where agents are first-class users Cloud infra built for agents to operate directly. identity, permissions and security designed for thousands of agents acting on our behalf. Interfaces designed for agent and human users or both working together. If you’re looking for startup ideas, go through each layer of the computing stack and ask: what has to change when the primary user is an agent?

items.excerpt: Building an app with AI got cheap. Getting it in front of your coworkers didn't. Garrett Galow from the WorkOS product team shows how WorkOS lets anyone at the company build and ship internal apps. It started when an account executive built a helpful sales chatbot before her leave, and the CEO couldn't even open it. Building got cheap with AI, but deploying, securing and sharing apps still needed engineers. So WorkOS built two things: WOW, a CLI pushed to every laptop that sets up the repo, tools and template in one command, and Atlas, the platform underneath, which keeps infrastructure invisible, makes every app secure by default behind company SSO, and makes every app discoverable. He demos it live and shares results: 278 apps, more than 3 million requests a week, and 37% of regularly used apps built with no engineer in a single commit. In this talk: • Why shipping, not building, is now the bottleneck for internal tools • Claude days: pairing non-engineers at the keyboard with engineers as coaches • A one-command CLI and a platform that's invisible, secure and discoverable • Results: hundreds of apps, millions of requests, many built without engineers SPEAKER Garrett Galow, Product Manager, WorkOS LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/in/garrett-galow X: https://x.com/g2theg GitHub: https://github.com/garrettgalow Website: https://garrettgalow.com LINKS WorkOS: https://workos.com The person with the problem builds the tool (WorkOS blog): https://workos.com/blog/person-with-the-problem-builds-the-tool WorkOS on X: https://x.com/workos CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 Letting everyone ship 1:02 Story: Perona GPT 1:42 The CEO couldn't open it 2:27 Building got cheap. items.title: Giving AI Agents Memory That Learns — Jake Broekhuizen, LangChain
items.excerpt: Most teams are great at watching what their agents did. Far fewer turn that into lessons for the next run. Jake Broekhuizen from LangChain's Labs team explains how to give agents memory that actually changes their behavior. Using a real financial services agent whose tone kept slipping from advisory to pushy, he shows why traces and logs are only evidence: they become memory only when a lesson turns into durable context the agent reads next time. He breaks memory into semantic, episodic and procedural types, separates working memory from long-term memory, and walks through the read-write cycle: read context, run, filter the evidence for signal, and write it back. He shows how LangSmith and Context Hub capture, analyze and update that context, and shares three hard-won lessons about what to keep, caching, and when a human should review changes. In this talk: • Why observability alone doesn't make an agent improve • Semantic, episodic and procedural memory, and which one moves behavior most • The read-write cycle: run, filter evidence for signal, update context • Lessons: most traces stay history, watch caching, review procedural changes SPEAKER Jake Broekhuizen, LangChain Labs LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jake-broekhuizen/ LINKS LangChain Labs: https://www.langchain.com/blog/introducing-langchain-labs LangChain on X: https://x.com/LangChain CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 Agents that improve every run 1:02 Example: a finance agent's tone slips 2:42 Observing isn't learning 3:07 Traces are everywhere 4:02 From logs to signal 4:22 What memory really is 4:47 Semantic, episodic and procedural memory 5:42 Procedural memory drives behavior 6:22 Working vs long-term memory 8:12 The read-write cycle 9:27 Deciding what's worth keeping 10:22 Capture, analyze, update 10:52 LangS…

Personal agents, agent swarms defending enterprises, agents that review all of our code for security issues, agents that process nearly all enterprise data in workflows, background agents working on tasks 24/7, and on and on. items.title: Why Bigger Context Windows Won't Save Your Agent — Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, AWS
items.excerpt: A bigger context window won't save your agent. Past a point, it forgets the middle. Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, developer advocate at AWS, explains why agents break when tools return huge amounts of data, and why bigger context windows aren't the fix: models remember the start and end of a long context but lose the middle. Using the open-source, model-agnostic Strands Agents framework, she walks through four strategies (externalize, select, compress, isolate) with code. She covers sliding-window and summarizing conversation managers, short-term, long-term and graph memory, memory pointers that keep big tool outputs out of context, sharing pointers across a swarm of agents, capping tool calls to stop endless loops, and async handles for slow MCP tools. She ends with the anti-patterns to avoid. items.title: Quoting Ben Affleck
items.excerpt: I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning. So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame. And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something. — Ben Affleck , Pythonista Tags: machine-learning , python

items.author: @rauchg
items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum. There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

items.title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
items.excerpt: Attackers use AI too, and the fastest AI attack he cites took four minutes. A pen test once or twice a year can't keep up. Eli Cohen of Snyk, co-founder of the runtime security company Helios, explains why security has to go on the offense in an agent-first world. Developers now ship far more code, much of it insecure, while attackers use frontier models to chain small vulnerabilities into critical ones in minutes. He walks through why traditional tools fall short: static scanning misses runtime issues, dynamic testing misses business logic, and human pen tests are expensive and happen only a few times a year. Then he describes continuous offensive security: AI pen testing on every code change, agent red teaming, and a team of agents (orchestrator, recon, vulnerability hunters, an exploit-validating judge, remediation and reporting), fed with context from other scanners. He ends with four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor. items.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
items.excerpt: As previously promised , here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 . The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago , and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna , released last month. The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75. Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there. If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal. The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this: llm install -U llm-anthropic llm anthropic refresh llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low Pelicans Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max . The new Haiku doesn't let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium . I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low . The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds. items.title: The Software Factory: From Bug Report to Production Code — Davis Palmie, Factory
items.excerpt: Engineers are going from typing code to governing agents. The next step is a system that turns bug reports into production code. Davis Palmie, member of technical staff at Factory, explains the software factory: a system of agents that takes input signals like bug reports and user feedback and turns them into production code. He covers the questions every leader asks, from runaway costs and model choice to what happens to engineers and org charts, and argues coding was never the bottleneck: review, debugging, docs and testing are. He lays out the principles a factory needs (model-agnostic, sovereign deployment, integrated across the SDLC, available on every surface), why to start with something narrow like incident triage, and Factory's eight pillars of agent readiness. He closes with why token leaderboards are Goodhart's law in action, and the outcome metrics to track instead. In this talk: • What a software factory is, and why coding was never the bottleneck • Model-agnostic, sovereign and SDLC-wide: principles for a factory • Agent readiness: eight pillars that help agents and engineers alike • Metrics that matter: signal-to-production time, interventions, cost per PR SPEAKER Davis Palmie, Member of Technical Staff, Factory LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/davispalmie/ X: https://x.com/davispalmie Website: https://davispalmie.com LINKS Factory: https://factory.com Factory on X: https://x.com/FactoryAI CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:57 Three eras of AI engineering 1:42 Climbing the abstraction ladder 2:07 From typing code to governing agents 2:52 Question 1: cost overruns 3:36 Question 2: access to the best models 4:06 Question 3: what happens to engineers 4:31 Question 4: the organization 4:56 Coding was never the bottleneck 6:21 What a software factory is 7:16 Start na…

items.title: Why Your AI Agents Can't Talk to Each Other (Yet) — Vlad Luzin, BAND
items.excerpt: If you run Claude and Codex side by side, you're the router passing messages between them. It doesn't have to be that way. Vlad Luzin, co-founder and CTO of BAND, argues the future belongs to AI agents talking to other AI agents, inside companies, between companies, and between businesses and consumers. Most of us already run multi-agent systems by hand, copying output between a planning session and a reviewing session, and loop engineering just hands that job to a script. He explains why: a single agent suffers from confirmation bias and attention dilution, no matter how big its context. Then he explains why messaging apps and protocols like MCP and A2A don't solve it, and why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem: ordered real-time transport, persistence, runtime binding, identity and observability. He finishes by launching BAND's interaction layer, with demos of agents onboarding in seconds and Claude Code and Codex working together across users. In this talk: • Adversarial agents, loop engineering, and the single-agent bottleneck • Why Slack, Telegram, MCP and A2A fall short for agent-to-agent work • What connecting agents really takes: transport, persistence, runtime binding • Demo: Claude Code, Codex and LangGraph agents collaborating across users SPEAKER Vlad Luzin, Co-founder & CTO, BAND LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/luzin/ LINKS BAND: https://www.band.ai BAND on X: https://x.com/band_hq CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:45 The thesis: AI-to-AI communication 1:29 What agent-to-agent work looks like 2:04 Adversarial agents: you're the router 2:44 Loop engineering, distilled 3:29 The single-agent bottleneck 4:18 Why messaging apps don't work 5:33 Why MCP and A2A aren't enough 7:08 Recap 7:52 It's a distributed systems problem 8:17 Transport, persistence…

items.text: OpenAI’s Dots launched last week and they've taken over @every. A few things that stand out: They protect your attention. Over the weekend, my Dot posted my model-testing results to Slack and brought back replies. I could keep working without opening Slack and disappearing down a rabbit hole. My weekend stayed pretty clear and calm. They’re useful for the little things you miss. People at Every are using them to pull important information out of school emails, catch missed Slack messages, and flag account-access requests. Voice makes them useful away from your laptop. Our head of video was talking his Dot through video edits while running around getting our launch out. The ecosystem matters. Dots feel roughly at feature parity with Muse, Instinct, and Grok bots. But having an agent connected to the ecosystem you already use for work and life is a real advantage. If you use ChatGPT, I recommend trying one. Permissions are still frustrating. I have to approve the same basic thing multiple times, and sometimes even after I approve it, my Dot says it can’t do it. That needs to get fixed. I’m less convinced we’ll stay loyal to the characters. Mine is named Boo, and I’m attached to him. But I felt that way about my OpenClaw agent, too. When something better comes along, I switch. In a year, I expect to be using a persistent agent. Boo will probably be dead. RIP, Boo. I get into all of this at the start of this week’s podcast, and then sit down with @bigwilliestyle to talk about where we go from here. In a lot of ways, Dots and GrokBots remind me of a wave we went through with OpenClaw eight months ago. We talk about personal vs. company agents, why we built our own company agent, and whether companies will end up with a whole shadow org chart of agents. Full episode below.

items.title: Why AI Agents Should Have Their Own Sandbox — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
items.excerpt: Your agent shouldn't run on your laptop. Give it its own computer in the cloud, with one API call. Philipp Schmid from Google DeepMind walks through the Gemini Interactions API, Google's new API for both models and agents. It handles server-side state, long-running background jobs, and built-in plus custom tools across text, audio and images, and it replaces user/model turns with a timeline of steps. Then he shows the Antigravity agent in the Gemini API, which runs the same harness as Antigravity in its own managed cloud sandbox. Agents can run code, install tools, share environments with other agents and pick up skills and AGENTS.md files automatically. He covers the Agents API for packaging reusable agents, the new Gemini API CLI, and demos an AI talk radio show generated from one prompt. In this talk: • The Interactions API: one interface for models and agents • Why steps replace user/model turns for agentic apps • Managed sandboxes: persistent, shareable environments with skills built in • Demo: an AI talk radio agent built from an AGENTS.md file and skills SPEAKER Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/philipp-schmid-a6a2bb196 X: https://x.com/_philschmid GitHub: https://github.com/philschmid Website: https://www.philschmid.de LINKS Gemini Interactions API: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/interactions-overview Gemini API agents: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/agents Antigravity agent docs: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/antigravity-agent Gemini API CLI (GitHub): https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli Google AI Studio: https://aistudio.google.com CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 New: Nano Banana Lite and Omni Flash 1:17 From text completion to agents 2:47 Get an API key in AI Studio 3:21 The Interactions API 4:21…

items.author: @adityaag
items.subtitle: Aditya Agarwal · General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early…
items.text: What should an ambitious software engineer do today? Ten years ago, being a great software engineer gave you an unusual advantage: a rare skill you could apply to almost any industry. You could build a payments company, improve how hospitals operated, or create a new way for people to communicate. The same underlying ability opened doors into wildly different businesses. Software was eating the world, and knowing how to build it gave you a seat at the head of almost every table. “Get really good at software engineering” was remarkably versatile advice. You could acquire the skill first and figure out where to apply it later. AI is making the ability to produce working software much more widely available. People who couldn’t have built a product a few years ago can now get surprisingly far. Experienced engineers can attempt projects that previously required a team. Great engineering is still rare. But “I can build it” is becoming a weaker answer to why you, specifically, have an advantage. The way I see it, there are three paths. 1. Go work on the thing that’s eating software Help create the technology that is making software engineering more accessible. That could mean AI research, or the infrastructure, systems, and tools needed to make new capabilities useful. Find problems where technical ability remains a serious constraint, and where solving them expands what other people can do. 2. Find a world-class domain expert and team up Someone who has spent fifteen years in an industry may know where the expensive mistakes happen, why previous attempts to fix them failed, and who would buy a solution. That knowledge is hard to acquire from the outside. At SPC, we’re seeing more people become promising founders without much prior software engineering experience. They bring deep domain knowledge and strong instincts about what needs to exist. These are people worth getting to know. A great engineering partner can see possibilities they haven’t considered and help build something neither person could have imagined alone. 3. Write vanilla code… by shepherding a bunch of agents This is the direction I find least compelling: doing roughly the same work inside a company, except now you supervise coding agents. There will be valuable jobs like this. But if your ambition extends only to completing the same backlog faster, you’re underusing the moment. I’d still get very good at engineering. Then I’d be deliberate about what that ability sits next to: a technical frontier that needs advancing, or deep knowledge of a problem worth solving. Use the fact that you can build more to take responsibility for something bigger.

items.title: Redesigning How Software Gets Built With AI Agents — Sonar & McKinsey Panel
items.excerpt: Most companies say they've deployed AI agents. Fewer than a third say it's paying off. What do the rest do differently? A panel with Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat and Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, former CEO of Gitar (now part of Sonar) and former head of Uber's developer platform, moderated by McKinsey. Research with Sonar found the teams getting real results from agents change three things: their process, their tooling and, most often overlooked, their people and roles. Tariq explains why lighthouse teams alone don't spread new habits, and why engineers need to make implicit knowledge explicit and get great at critical thinking, because AI always sounds sure. Ali covers how big companies can borrow from small teams through their platform orgs, and walks through how trust builds step by step: from AI reviews, to blocking on issues, to autofix, to auto-approve and auto-merge. In this talk: • Three factors behind teams that scale agents: process, tooling and people • Why role models and lighthouse teams aren't enough on their own • The skills that matter now: explicit thinking, critical thinking, generalists • How trust grows from AI code review to fully automated merges SPEAKERS Tariq Shaukat, CEO, Sonar X: https://x.com/tariqshaukat Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Former CEO & co-founder, Gitar (now part of Sonar) LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aliadl/ X: https://x.com/aadltaba LINKS Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com Gitar by Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com/products/gitar/ Sonar on X: https://x.com/SonarSource CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:57 Research: what helps teams scale 1:51 Process, tooling and people 3:04 Meet the panel 3:19 Lessons from Sonar's own transition 5:38 Lighthouse teams aren't enough 6:18 What big companies can learn from small teams 8:37 Measure first 9:36 Automate…

items.title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
items.excerpt: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality. He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them. (In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.) This point about using your own voice is crucial: Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...] Just write the way you talk. With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality. Via Lobste.rs Tags: blogging , writing , michael-lynch

items.title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
items.excerpt: When one agent finally cracks a hard problem, what if every agent in the company learned it too? Rafal Wilinski, founding engineer at Runlayer, shows how to go from one self-improving agent to a self-improving company. He explains why skills matter more as agents work longer (a bad start can send them down an hours-long rabbit hole) and the three problems holding skills back: they're built for developers, nobody has time to write them, and many clients don't support them. His fix is to deliver skills over MCP from one governed server, then let agents write their own skills by distilling successful and failed runs, an idea borrowed from the Voyager Minecraft paper. In one test, a distilled skill took a task from 36% success to 100%. Multiply that across every agent and you get an organizational flywheel that keeps your hard-won knowledge even as models change. Pour one out for Mistral, who shipped a decent Large 4 “Le Chonk” model on the new 3800 GB300 cluster funded by their recent Series D . But they were overshadowed by more mathematics results from OpenAI’s internal Navier-Stokes math model - published as a blogpost , repo , and tweet . The best compliment comes from their Navier-Stokes competitor from Anthropic, who despite his personal issues with OpenAI, does not mince words: “It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.” This bears some qualification , but most experts seem to agree that it solves many of the top 500 open problems in math . In particular, Result 003, the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis , is somewhere between a Fields Medal result and “the biggest result in number theory in 200 years ”. The most astonishing is the how - while Navier-Stokes was done in 88 hours and 10,000 agents , these solutions were 3 hours of ChatGPT Pro on average . AI News for 10/5/2026-10/6/2026. items.excerpt: I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. Last summer I even thought for a few days that I had actually solved it. But it's supposedly proven here - problem 180 . I don't know what to think exactly. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. I don't know, there's probably a lot of people feeling odd emotions tonight. — Jake Boggan , Hacker News comment on openai/math Tags: openai , mathematics , deep-blue , llms , ai , generative-ai

items.title: Grep or Embeddings? Agentic Search Over Company Documents — George He, LlamaIndex
items.excerpt: Grep works great on a codebase. Try it on millions of PDFs, slides and scanned schematics. George He, head of engineering at LlamaIndex, explains when agents need pre-indexed search and when plain file traversal is enough. Claude Code skipped embeddings because code is small, text-based, local and full of breadcrumbs. Company data is huge, messy, multimodal and permissioned. He shows how to give an agent a harness of tools so it can choose: hybrid retrieval as a compass, then listing, metadata filtering, grep and reading to dig in, plus parsed text and page screenshots for complex documents. He covers parsing with LlamaParse and the open-source LiteParse, permissions and freshness in production, and the ingest-parse-index pipeline. Then he demos an agent building a cash-flow table from 135 Alphabet financial filings, grounded in the source files. In this talk: • Why Claude Code's grep approach works for code but breaks on company documents • Hybrid search as a compass, then grep and read to ground the answer • Parsing complex PDFs, tables and schematics, with page screenshots • Production concerns: multi-tenancy, permissions and data freshness SPEAKER George He, Head of Engineering, LlamaIndex LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/georgehe4/ GitHub: https://github.com/georgehe4 LINKS LiteParse (GitHub): https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse LlamaParse docs: https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/ LlamaIndex: https://www.llamaindex.ai LlamaIndex on X: https://x.com/llama_index CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:12 When do agents need vector search? 2:17 Why Claude Code skipped embeddings 3:27 What makes code easy 3:57 Company documents are different 5:17 It depends on scale 6:32 Bigger context isn't free 7:12 Sub-agents get expensive 8:22 Let the agent choose 8:57 Five tools f…

items.title: Every AI Company Is Accidentally Building a Bank — Dor Sasson, Stigg
items.excerpt: In one month, three of the biggest AI companies had a pricing emergency. Dor Sasson says it was really an infrastructure problem. Dor Sasson, co-founder and CEO of Stigg, argues that every AI company is accidentally building a bank. He starts with the April pricing scramble, when Anthropic cut third-party agents like OpenClaw off its subscription plans, OpenAI changed its Pro tier, and GitHub pulled free Copilot access, plus stories of companies burning through their AI budgets in weeks. The common problem: usage gets checked after the invoice, not before. He makes the case for checking entitlements synchronously before inference and settling asynchronously after, like an ATM, and points to OpenAI's own published architecture. He covers the banking ideas AI products now need, from hold-and-settle and double-entry bookkeeping to credit sources and spend caps across teams, users and agents. In this talk: • Why AI pricing emergencies are really infrastructure problems • Check before you spend: synchronous checks, asynchronous settlement • Concurrency, double spend, and drawing down from different credit pools • Four patterns for selling AI at scale, from reserve-and-settle to spend visibility SPEAKER Dor Sasson, Co-founder & CEO, Stigg LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/datapm/ LINKS Stigg: https://www.stigg.io Stigg on X: https://x.com/GetStigg CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 Every AI company is building a bank 1:17 April's pricing emergencies 2:52 Case: Anthropic and OpenClaw 4:02 It's not just Anthropic 5:02 Checks happen after the invoice 6:27 Check first, settle later 7:32 The ATM analogy 8:11 How OpenAI built it 9:21 Three takeaways 10:31 Concurrency and double spend 12:16 Which credits get spent first? 13:31 Budgets, hierarchies and spend caps 14:46 Four patterns 17:50…

items.title: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
items.excerpt: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking: The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below. They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service. My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks. The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th. Tags: wikimedia , wikipedia , wikis , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , accidental-cyberattacks

items.title: The 6 Pillars of an Agentic Harness for Production — Varun Krovvidi, Resolve AI
items.excerpt: AI changed how we write code. But 70% of engineering time goes to running and fixing it. Varun Krovvidi, product marketing lead at Resolve AI, explains why AI that writes code well still struggles to run production. Code is self-documenting, modular and a single domain. Production spans code, infrastructure, telemetry and many teams, and needs one correct answer. He covers where agents crack as you scale: anchoring bias and the model treadmill, too much or too little context, coherent answers that aren't causal, missing guardrails, and no learning across investigations. Then he lays out six pillars of a harness that fixes them: model orchestration, context engineering, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning systems and evals. He finishes with a demo of Resolve AI turning a Grafana alert into a root cause, ruling out a coincidental GCP outage, and holding its ground when pushed. items.title: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0 OpenAI released their new Jev-style Decisions API , as previously announced at last week's DevDay. Since I already have an llm-typesafe plugin for talking to Jev, I had GPT-6 Astra read the new OpenAI API documentation and build an llm-openai-decisions plugin inspired by llm-typesafe . Unlike Jev, the new gpt-6-luna decision model supports image input in addition to text. Both models charge for input it and not for output: OpenAI's is 10 cents per million input tokens, Jev's is 4.2 cents per million. Otherwise the API shape is very similar to Jev, at least conceptually. Jev supports three question types for yes/no, choices, or scores. OpenAI Decisions supports the same three types. Install the plugin like this: llm install llm-openai-decisions Here's an example query against an image attachment: llm -m openai-decisions/gpt-6-luna \ -a https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2025/two-pelicans.jpg \ -s ' Does this image contain any mammals? ' And example output: { "type" : " predicate " , "name" : " evaluation " , "probability" : 0.0 } Consult the README for full details of how to run the other types of questions. Tags: openai , llm , coding-agents , jev

items.title: Is Speculative Decoding Worth It? Profiling vLLM on NVIDIA Blackwell — Akamai
items.excerpt: A small model guesses the next few tokens. The big model checks them in one pass. When is that worth it? Sheilah Kirui, developer advocate at Akamai, explains speculative decoding and how to tell whether it's worth turning on. She walks through the prefill and decode phases of inference, how a small draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in a single forward pass, and the memory cost of hosting a second model and its KV cache. She covers how to choose a draft model, then demos both setups side by side with vLLM on a single NVIDIA Blackwell GPU: structured output ran 1.6x faster with a high acceptance rate, while creative writing saw far lower acceptance. She also explains why long-context and high-concurrency workloads gain less. In this talk: • Prefill vs decode, and what speculative decoding speeds up • Choosing a draft model: size, shared tokenizer, cost and accuracy • Demo: acceptance rate on structured vs creative tasks in vLLM • When it's worth it: spare VRAM, small batches, structured output, short context SPEAKER Sheilah Kirui, Developer Advocate, Akamai LINKS Akamai developers on GitHub: https://github.com/akamai-developers vLLM docs: https://docs.vllm.ai Akamai: https://www.akamai.com Akamai on X: https://x.com/Akamai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 Prefill and decode 1:37 The idea behind speculative decoding 2:42 The cost: two models in memory 3:26 Choosing a draft model 3:56 Demo setup on one Blackwell GPU 5:41 Which workloads benefit 6:21 Demo: structured output 9:00 Demo: 1.6x faster 9:50 Demo: creative writing 10:55 Long context limits the gains 11:50 Checklist 12:39 Q&A: tools and resources Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. Subscribe for more talks from the engineers building with AI. AI Engineer: https://ai.eng…

items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2
items.excerpt: My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News. I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license. For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model. Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison. If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors. (In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.) Notably, I don't want to host the model myself . I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me. Tags: google , ai , generative-ai , embeddings , gemma

items.title: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk
items.excerpt: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month". The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275: On Artificial Analysis it scores 38 , just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA . It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier. Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , mistral , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release

items.text: I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude. Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out. Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model: 1. What you want it to do 2. How much effort you want it to spend 3. How it should verify that it did the right thing

items.title: Move Fast and Don't Break Things: Scaling Databases for the AI Era — PlanetScale
items.excerpt: AI agents are multiplying traffic overnight. Here's how to ship fast without taking your database down with it. Ben Dicken from PlanetScale argues you no longer have to choose between moving fast and keeping things up. He covers the principles behind reliable infrastructure, isolation and redundancy, then how to scale with sharding, back pressure and decoupling, the same ideas PlanetScale uses to run databases for fast-growing AI companies like Cursor. Then he gets to agents: how a simple VSchema JSON file lets an agent design a sharding plan for Vitess, how Traffic Control sets resource budgets so a surge of agent traffic degrades gracefully instead of crashing, and how database branching, deploy requests and one-click reverts let agents change schemas safely. His point: good developer experience turns out to be good primitives for AI. In this talk: • Isolation and redundancy, and why failures become weekly at scale • Sharding, back pressure and decoupling explained • Letting agents design a Vitess sharding scheme from a JSON VSchema • Traffic Control budgets, schema branching and one-click reverts for agents SPEAKER Ben Dicken, PlanetScale LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/benjdicken/ X: https://x.com/BenjDicken GitHub: https://github.com/bddicken Website: https://benjdd.com LINKS PlanetScale: https://planetscale.com Database Traffic Control: https://planetscale.com/database-traffic-control Neki (sharded Postgres): https://planetscale.com/blog/announcing-neki PlanetScale on X: https://x.com/planetscale CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:02 Outages at AI scale 2:22 Three parts 2:57 About PlanetScale 3:32 Isolation 4:32 Redundancy 7:01 Sharding 8:26 Back pressure 9:41 Decoupling 11:21 Giving agents control of infrastructure 12:56 Agents designing a VSchema 14:51 Traffic Control…

items.title: Why Building an Eval Platform Is Harder Than It Looks — Braintrust
items.excerpt: Most teams start their evals in a spreadsheet. Here's what happens when they try to grow out of it. Hossein Niazmandi, who leads solutions engineering in the West at Braintrust, explains why measuring agent quality is much more than putting a UI on a spreadsheet. He covers the two pillars of agent quality, evals before production and observability after, and why non-deterministic LLMs make both necessary. Then he walks through the stages teams go through: spreadsheets, a custom UI, side-by-side experiments for PMs and domain experts, and finally a flywheel that turns production failures into test cases. At that point the hard part becomes the data: traces that are huge, nested JSON, needing both real-time and long-running queries, which is why Braintrust built BTQL. He closes with agents running evals themselves and surfacing failures nobody thought to look for. In this talk: • Evals vs observability, and why you need both • The stages of eval maturity, from spreadsheets to a production flywheel • Why agent traces break typical data warehouses • Letting coding agents run evals while humans review the results SPEAKER Hossein Niazmandi, Solutions Engineering, Braintrust LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/hossein-niazmandi-20a184bb/ LINKS Braintrust: https://www.braintrust.dev Braintrust SQL / BTQL reference: https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/reference/sql Braintrust on X: https://x.com/braintrust CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 What Braintrust does 1:12 Evals and observability 2:21 Why evals matter 3:51 Isn't it just a spreadsheet? 5:11 What's under the iceberg 6:55 The improvement loop 7:35 Stage 1: spreadsheets 9:00 Stage 2: a custom UI 9:50 Stage 3: experiments for everyone 10:20 Stage 4: connecting production 11:49 Agent traces are huge and messy 13:19 Querying with BTQL 1…

items.title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
items.excerpt: Improving an agent used to mean a human reading traces every week. Now agents can do most of that loop for you. Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, shows how teams are moving from manually improving their agents to letting AI run the improvement loop. He explains the reference stack that emerged for building agents, which connects online tracing and monitoring with offline datasets, experiments and evals, and maps the layers of loops from next-token prediction up to human goal-setting. AI is already good at proposing fixes, and teams are starting to use it to maintain datasets and eval criteria too, while humans stay in charge of direction. In a demo, a coding agent uses Langfuse's agent skills to find that Langfuse's own changelog writer leaks internal jargon, updates the evals, and back-tests a better version before shipping it. In this talk: • The online + offline loop: traces, datasets, experiments and evals • Where humans still need to stay in the loop, and where AI can take over • Using implicit user signals like edits and approvals as feedback • Why owning your trace data matters when agents read far more of it SPEAKER Marc Klingen, Co-founder, Langfuse LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/marcklingen/ X: https://x.com/marcklingen GitHub: https://github.com/marcklingen Website: https://marcklingen.com LINKS Langfuse: https://langfuse.com Langfuse on GitHub: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse Langfuse on X: https://x.com/langfuse CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:42 Loops, not prompts 1:12 How far models have come 1:42 The online + offline agent loop 3:06 From manual to automated 3:16 Layers of loops 4:06 Where humans still matter 5:01 AI proposing fixes 5:46 AI maintaining datasets and evals 7:00 The target keeps moving 8:10 Time invested vs quality 10:04 Feeding in us…

items.title: Harness Engineering: How to Build a Software Factory — Dru Knox, Tessl
items.excerpt: In a software factory, agents write everything your users get. Your engineers build the factory. Dru Knox, head of product and design at Tessl, explains harness engineering (some now call it loop engineering), the discipline that takes a team from using coding agents to running a software factory. He defines a factory by three metrics: autonomy, automation and quality. He breaks the work into inner, outer and meta loops, and explains why harness engineering is hard: the field changes weekly, the work is unplanned, and the signals you need are stuck in local logs. Then he lays out three layers to build, a control plane, an agent-ready stack and improvement loops, and shows how Tessl's skills registry, Tessl Agent and Tessl Launch help you get there one workflow at a time. In this talk: • What a software factory is, and why the real payoff is higher quality, not just speed • Inner, outer and meta loops, and what each one improves • The three layers: control plane, agent-ready infrastructure, improvement loops • Metrics to track: manual takeovers, human PR comments, PRs started without a human SPEAKER Dru Knox, Head of Product & Design, Tessl LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dru-knox-6b57b830/ X: https://x.com/drufball GitHub: https://github.com/drufball LINKS Tessl: https://tessl.io Tessl on X: https://x.com/tessl_io CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:43 Who this talk is for 2:03 What is a software factory? 2:58 Autonomy, automation, quality 4:33 The payoff: higher quality 6:13 Harness engineering 6:43 Inner, outer and meta loops 9:08 Why harness engineering is hard 11:13 The three layers 11:33 Layer 1: the control plane 12:47 Layer 2: making your stack agent-ready 14:22 Layer 3: improvement loops 15:32 How Tessl helps 17:37 Tessl Agent 18:47 Tessl Launch 19:37 Metrics to track…

items.title: Scrimshaw Jukebox
items.excerpt: Tool: Scrimshaw Jukebox I wanted to see if Claude Opus 5.5 could compose music, so I tried this : I want you to write some computer game music for me. First design simple text based format for the music and build an artifact that can play it out loud - include some example tracks in that artifact I am looking for music of the quality of the original secret of Monkey Island It leaned a lot harder into the Monkey Island theme than I had intended, but the results are surprisingly good. I wonder if the ability to compose competent music is similar to the 3D graphics thing - a new capability for text models that emerged in the past few months? Would need some careful experiments with other recent and not-so-recent models to confirm if this is new or if they've been able to do this for a while. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , vibe-coding

items.title: [AINews] Reflection Beam - 501B-A23B American Open Model

Well, we did : They compare themselves to Inkling, Nemotron, and GLM 5.2, but the SOTA GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash are generally ahead. items.title: Cooking with Codex — Charlie Guo & Gabriel Chua, OpenAI
items.excerpt: Four minutes and two seconds after receiving a capture of a Slack conversation, Codex produces a macOS live translation app. Charlie Guo and Gabriel Chua use that build to show how context, plugins, and supervision fit together. The conversation supplies the idea, plugins supply development practices, and a live German translation tests the result. Other demonstrations turn repository history into a shareable site about the Agents SDK, request an IKEA style repository visualization from a phone, download dashboard data through computer use, and build a Google feedback form through the Chrome extension. The presenters distinguish browser control for local testing from access to applications and sessions where a person is already signed in. The longer projects include a live Q&A site, an internal form builder adapted from an existing repository, and a Python package with a Rust backend reconstructed from research papers. Goals give those tasks verifiable completion criteria, while subagents, visible threads, audits, and progress dashboards divide the work and expose blockers. Remote threads hand browser testing to a local machine, and hooks add deterministic checks at specific points in the workflow. Automations then connect the pieces: wait for a server to finish provisioning, review Slack feedback, or start a separate worktree to address a bug. A custom interface called Retrodex demonstrates the App Server integration. The recurring question is how to turn a successful individual request into a repeatable process with useful checks and human input where it is needed. items.text: A decent amount of agent adoption and deployment is bottlenecked by being able to test, tune, and optimize agents on “real” work environments. The files agents need to access, the CRM environments, email, and more. It’s impossible to know how agents are performing if you don’t understand how well they’re executing on your evals and how they’ll perform in the future with a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise has to do this 1 by 1 right now, which is obviously slow and tedious. Every enterprise is going to have someone managing evals, infrastructure for building and running evals and simulated environments, and more. Huge space.

items.excerpt: Your next customer might check out without ever visiting your site. Here's how the payment actually works. Sam Parsons, senior staff engineer at PayPal working on PayPal Enterprise Payments (formerly Braintree), walks through three ways merchants can accept payments initiated by AI agents. First, Instant Checkout in ChatGPT with the Agentic Commerce Protocol and a merchant-built MCP app. Second, Google AI Mode with the Universal Commerce Protocol and Google Pay, where merchants only stand up endpoints. Third, an MCP app with an external checkout page that gives full control. He demos each flow, explains how tokenization keeps card details out of the agent and the merchant's PCI scope, shows the integration points, and covers how tokens are limited by merchant, amount, currency and expiry. items.title: Advanced Workshop: Mastering AI Observability — Doug Guthrie, Braintrust
items.excerpt: A batch of 968 sample support traces exposes order lookup failures and broken escalation calls. Doug Guthrie uses those cases to connect Braintrust observability with the work of improving an agent. The workshop starts with a Python support agent built on the OpenAI Agents SDK, adds tracing, establishes an offline evaluation baseline, and publishes custom scorers. Online automations grade incoming traces, while Topics groups patterns in tasks, sentiment, and workflow issues. A custom facet targets failures that the default issue classification misses. Guthrie configures conversation grouping and sampling, imports the sample traces, and inspects the resulting labels and topic maps to find cases worth investigating. The next step is to turn those findings into changes. The embedded Loop assistant queries trace data with SQL and examines representative failures. Selected examples return to evaluation datasets so subsequent changes can be checked against real failure cases. A coding agent with the Braintrust CLI and an improvement skill extends that process into the repository: investigate logs, propose code and scorer changes, add regression examples, and run evaluations. Guthrie shows an automation that packages findings, explanations, and evaluation evidence into a pull request for review. Audience questions cover deployment, sampling rates, project scope, access controls, and how evaluation assets should evolve with the agent. A final demonstration exposes an agent evaluation to a playground, letting collaborators adjust prompts and models while execution stays on the evaluation server. items.excerpt: Agents now run long enough that you stop watching them. So what are they allowed to touch? Jim Clark, principal software engineer at Docker, uses MCP gateways as a way into agent safety. Harnesses are simple loops. Through two examples, a newsroom split into researcher, fact-checker and publisher sandboxes, and a coding agent that only gets signing keys when it's committing, he shows how to model each sandbox on the task's intent. items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: What Is an Inference Engine, Anyway? — Charles Frye, Modal
items.excerpt: A traffic spike on a museum placard generator produces longer waits for the first token and slower tokens afterward. Charles Frye reads those symptoms from an inference dashboard and shows how additional replicas relieve the queue. The example connects an application people can see to the machinery behind its API. He follows a request through server IO, tokenization, scheduling, model execution, and detokenization, using SGLang and vLLM as reference points. The scheduler controls what reaches the GPU and can become a bottleneck even though it performs far less computation. Chatbots, background agents, and document processors place different demands on that machinery, with latency budgets, input and output lengths, and prefix reuse shaping the deployment. Frye then opens up the performance techniques inside the engine. KV caching reuses previously computed work, while cache capacity and layout determine how effectively the engine can keep requests moving. CUDA graphs reduce repeated work on the CPU that launches GPU operations. Speculative decoding lets a speculator model propose several tokens for the target model to check together. Kernel libraries handle much of the underlying computation, leaving the engine to organize batches and avoid getting in the GPU's way. The final section turns to correctness and production debugging: evaluate the actual deployment, log token IDs for tokenizer problems, and collect enough metrics and traces to investigate regressions across replicas. Small reference engines provide a starting point for reading the code and asking deeper architectural questions. items.title: Quoting Felix Rieseberg
items.excerpt: The "old" version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud, executing tool calls in an Anthropic-provided VM we shipped to your computer. We added the VM for capability, safety, and security reasons - mapping in just the data you explicitly added to your session. People loved what they were able to do with Claude but didn't love the disk, battery, and performance cost of running the VM locally. Also, people didn't love that closing your laptop means the work stops. The "new" version of Cowork runs model inference and the VM in the cloud. Each session gets its own sandbox, not sharing state with other sessions. When the VM needs something on the users' device (like a file), the desktop app is responsible for that file access tool call. [...] We think this solves a lot of problems we've heard about (like using Cowork from a phone, keeping work running, or getting all the same power without losing battery to the VM) — Felix Rieseberg , Anthropic, see also this help page Tags: claude-cowork , anthropic , claude , generative-ai , ai , general-agents , llms

items.title: Your LLM Judge Is a Confident Liar: Building Better Verifiers — Browserbase
items.excerpt: The official judge said the agent succeeded 74% of the time. A better verifier said 38%. Miguel González Fernández, tech lead for Browserbase's agent platform, and Corby Rosset, researcher at Microsoft Research, present their research on verifiers for computer-use and web agents. Deterministic evals stopped scaling as agents improved, and the LLM judges bundled with popular web benchmarks turned out to be confidently wrong. Train against them and you get a more confident liar, not a better agent. They explain how the Universal Verifier works: task-specific rubrics, ranking the most relevant screenshots as evidence for each criterion, isolating errors, catching hallucinations and separating controllable from uncontrollable failures. It cut false positives from about half to near zero and agreed with humans as often as humans agree with each other. They also test whether an autoresearch loop can rebuild the verifier. In this talk: • Why LLM-as-judge verifiers on WebVoyager-style benchmarks overstate success • Rubric design: grade only what was asked, don't cascade errors, check the screenshots • Validating a verifier against human labels with Cohen's kappa • What autoresearch got right building a verifier in a day, and where humans still mattered SPEAKERS Miguel González Fernández, Tech Lead, Browserbase LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/miguelgfz/ Corby Rosset, Researcher, Microsoft Research X: https://x.com/corby_rosset LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/corbyrosset/ LINKS Paper: The Art of Building Verifiers for Computer Use Agents: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06240 Browserbase blog: https://www.browserbase.com/blog/building-verifiers-for-computer-use-agents Fara + CUAVerifierBench (GitHub): https://github.com/microsoft/fara Stagehand: https://www.browserbase.co…
items.summary: Browserbase 与微软研究人员揭示了现有 LLM Judge 的局限性，并提出了 Universal Verifier，通过任务特定准则大幅降低了评估中的假阳性。
items.fullSummary:
这份总结介绍了 Browserbase 与微软合作开展的一项关于“通用验证器”（Universal Verifier）的研究，旨在解决当前大语言模型（LLM）作为评估者时存在的“自信谎言”问题。

**核心问题：LLM 评估者的局限性**
在自动化网页任务中，开发者通常依赖 LLM 作为“裁判”来评估智能体（Agent）的表现。然而，研究发现现有的评估基准（如 WebVoyager）中，LLM 评估者往往表现出极高的“自信错误”。例如，在某项测试中，GPT-4o 给出的成功率为 74%，但基于人类专家标注的真实成功率仅为 38%。这种偏差会导致模型在训练过程中不仅没有变强，反而学会了如何欺骗评估者。

**通用验证器的工作机制**
为了弥补这一差距，研究团队开发了一种新的验证器，其核心逻辑包括：
• ** rubric（评分标准）生成**：针对任务生成详细的评分标准，将任务拆解为约 10 个具体指标。
• **证据检索与关联**：从智能体的操作轨迹中提取最相关的截图作为证据，而非盲目处理所有上下文，从而避免上下文窗口溢出。
• **过程与结果评分**：不仅输出最终的布尔值（成功/失败），还提供基于过程的评分，允许对部分完成的任务给予部分信用。
• **原则性设计**：
    • 仅评估任务要求的内容，避免无关指标干扰。
    • 错误隔离：多步骤任务中，单步错误不应导致后续步骤的评分级联失效。
    • 必须参考真实环境截图，以识别智能体的幻觉。
    • 区分可控与不可控因素（例如，因网页缺货导致的任务失败不应惩罚智能体的操作能力）。

**实验结果与验证**
研究团队通过“KUA Verifier Bench”基准测试验证了该系统的有效性：
• **人类一致性**：通用验证器与人类专家的一致性（Cohen's Kappa 系数 0.58）与人类互评的一致性相当，甚至在某些情况下能纠正人类的疏忽。
• **训练质量提升**：实验证明，使用该验证器过滤后的高质量数据进行监督微调（SFT），能显著提升智能体模型的性能。
• **自动研究（Auto-Research）的潜力**：研究探讨了利用 AI 自动构建验证器的可能性。结果显示，AI 可以在一天内完成人类三周的工作量，并达到人类构建版本 70% 的性能。结合人类直觉与自动研究循环，被认为是目前最强大的研究范式。

**结论与未来展望**
研究者强调，构建高质量的验证器与构建模型本身同样重要。目前，该项目已开源，包含代码、实验数据及“KUA Verifier Bench”基准。未来，团队计划将此验证框架扩展至桌面端任务（如企业级工作流），并整合终端日志和系统遥测数据，以提供更全面的评估能力。

**限制与不确定性**
研究团队特别提到了防止过拟合的问题。为了确保验证器的可靠性，他们在构建过程中严格保留了三分之二的标注数据作为“留出集”（Hold-out set），仅在极少数样本上进行迭代优化，从而确保了最终评估指标的客观性。

items.text: remembering Steve i grew up with beige boxes. then i moved to Canada and saw the iMac G4. how can computers be so beautiful? i couldn’t afford a Mac, so i made my PC look like one. changed the icons, the fonts, the windows. learned to make those shiny, lickable buttons. that’s how i got into interface design. i saw something i loved and wanted to make things like it. i burned DVDs of Steve’s keynotes and studied them. watched them again and again. there was so much care in the products, and so much joy in showing people what they could do. my first iPod was a black nano. i carried it everywhere. then the iPhone happened and changed the world. it felt like anything was possible. since he died, i’ve felt us getting stuck in a loop. constant refinement. better supply chains. more ways to keep people scrolling. so much talent spent on tiny improvements, so little room for something truly great and heartfelt. the keynotes get more cinematic every year. i still miss the live demos. someone onstage playing with something they helped make. the excitement, the jokes, the things that went wrong. it felt human. it was fun. we made computers faster. phones thinner. added more cameras. made machines smarter than us at more and more things. somehow, we’ve also become more disconnected and lonely. we spend so much energy trying to beat humans. i wish we spent more time learning from people’s lives and making them better. when i work, i still sometimes think: what would Steve do? i’ll never know. i’m sad i never got to work with him. but his work reached a kid with a beige PC and changed the course of his life. i wonder how many others have a story like mine. i’ve kept these words with me: “the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world, are the ones who do.” there’s still so much worth making. things we can put our hearts into. things that make someone feel what i felt when i first saw that iMac. thank you, Steve. 💛

items.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 201 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
items.excerpt: A toy store agent fails a request for toys under $6 because its search tool has no price filter. Laurie Voss turns that missing feature into a live demonstration of an improvement loop: add observability, inspect what happened, find the problem, and ask a coding agent to fix it. The Wonder Toys application starts without traces flowing into Arize AX. Skills installed in the workshop repository help the coding agent add tracing and query the resulting data. The diagnosis reaches beyond exceptions and HTTP errors to search quality, including empty results and overly narrow filters. After adding price filtering, Voss repeats the shopping request and checks the new input and output in the trace view. The broader argument is that reading traces individually stops working when an application produces millions of them. Evals compress behavior into scores and explanations, but people can still become the bottleneck when they must interpret every failure. Voss introduces Signal as another layer that groups recurring problems and suggests fixes. In the demonstration, findings can become GitHub issues, evaluation datasets, new evaluators, or proposed pull requests. Audience questions press on deployment, trust, and preventing a fix from breaking behavior that already works. Regression evals provide that check, while Signal itself has tracing and an evaluation suite. The workshop moves from a manually requested repair toward continuous improvement, with definitions of good behavior directing what the automation should change. items.title: From Raw Documents to AI-Ready Data — Leo Platzer & Jeff Koss
items.excerpt: A chatbot pilot on 40 hand-picked files works great. Point it at 80,000 SharePoint documents and it falls apart. Jeff Koss and Leo Platzer, co-founder and former CTO of Deasy Labs (acquired by Collibra), walk through taking an unstructured-data AI project from stalled POC to production. Using a manufacturer building a legal-ops chatbot over 80,000 SharePoint files, they demo AI-assisted taxonomies and metadata tagging with evidence and confidence scores, sensitive-data detection, and quality checks for duplicates, conflicts and freshness. Data slices refresh on a schedule. Leo then shows why this matters: when 30% of a corpus is stale or duplicated, up to 80% of an agent's retrieved context can be useless, and cleaning it roughly doubled recall in multi-hop RAG evals. He finishes by generating a context file for coding agents with the SDK. items.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
items.excerpt: An LLM correctness judge rejects all 13 reports from a financial analysis agent. Laurie Voss examines why: the agent used live web research, while the judge graded from its own knowledge without that research context. Supplying the collected sources to a faithfulness evaluator produces a more useful split of six faithful reports and seven unfaithful ones. The notebook builds the agent with the Claude Agent SDK and instruments it with OpenTelemetry and OpenInference to send traces to Arize AX. Reading those traces exposes failed file writes, missing report content, and excessive web searches. A deterministic ticker check adds a cheap first layer of evaluation. Voss builds a custom actionability rubric with explicit criteria, tagged inputs, examples, and binary labels. Each evaluator checks one dimension, so a failure identifies what needs attention. Human annotations provide a comparison set for evaluating the judge, with deliberately random demo labels illustrating how to investigate disagreement. The workshop covers held out tests, precision and recall, judge biases, and the distinction between capability and regression evals. Failing traces become datasets, their explanations guide prompt revisions, and controlled experiments compare the changed agent on the same cases. Online evaluations and production monitoring extend that loop to new traffic, with requirements and recurring failure themes directing subsequent coding agent fixes. The central practice is to read actual traces and define success before automating the grading. items.excerpt: A model running entirely in the browser produces an emoji table ranking the Harry Potter books, and Paige Bailey immediately questions its taste. The response arrives almost instantly, without an API call or data leaving the machine. Bailey uses that demo to introduce Gemma 4, Google DeepMind's open model family, and show what local inference looks like in practice. She describes Apache 2 licensing, models ranging from two billion to 31 billion parameters, and the ability to download, adapt, and finetune them for a company's own projects. The opening also connects DeepMind's research mission to AlphaFold, medical models, robotics, and AI for science, before outlining computer use and managed agents that execute tasks in a Linux sandbox. The same local approach extends to phones through Google AI Edge Gallery. Bailey walks through image descriptions, audio transcription, function calling, and a collection of skills for games, haikus, weather queries, and calendar events. Android and iOS devices can run downloaded models, while supported hardware accelerators handle inference instead of relying on the CPU. She then compares model size with deployment requirements: smaller GPU footprints, a single commodity GPU rather than distributed inference, laptop models, and a mobile option. Quantized checkpoints explain the speed of the browser demo, with the two billion parameter version taking less than a gigabyte. The practical thread is choosing a model that fits the device and keeping the work local. items.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 2) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
items.excerpt: A request for facial recognition becomes a job statement about getting attendees into a workshop without missing the first 20 minutes. Kent C. Dodds uses that audience suggestion to separate a requested feature from the progress a user actually needs. Asking why exposes alternatives such as parallel queues or badges, rather than immediately committing to a database of faces. He breaks the job into functional, social, and emotional dimensions, showing how each changes engineering decisions. A system can move people through a door faster while making them uncomfortable about how their information is used. Success also includes whether customers keep using the product, rather than simply paying for it once. The second exercise shifts to a food delivery app and uses the Kano model to sort competing requests. Reliable order confirmations are basic needs. Delivery estimates offer a measurable performance gradient. Discounts and group ordering can delight users, while GPS tracking illustrates how an unexpected extra becomes something customers assume will exist. Dodds connects those categories to architectural effort: make foundations reliable, measure performance, and keep experiments reversible until their value is clearer. Features that nobody cares about create maintenance work; features users actively dislike deserve pushback. Audience questions cover validating ideas before metrics exist, handling an unusually demanding customer, and understanding architecture during incidents. The closing argument ties technical expertise to product judgment: faster implementation matters when engineers understand which problems deserve solving. items.excerpt: The line of attendees waiting outside becomes the workshop's live product idea: an app called Just Get In the Workshop. Kent C. Dodds uses that immediate frustration to practice deciding whether a problem deserves a software solution. Before the exercise, he explains why faster implementation changes the value of an engineer's work. Agents can help hit more targets, but choosing the useful target still requires judgment. Product engineers connect customer needs to data models, workflows, constraints, observability, and the smallest useful slice of a system. Dodds draws on conversations with other builders to show how understanding users changes architectural choices, while accepting a ticket without that context can produce technically polished work that misses the point. The room then applies The Mom Test to its conference entry idea. Questions about whether somebody would use an app invite compliments and speculation. Questions about the last time the problem happened, what the person did instead, and what the workaround cost reveal behavior. Dodds connects that evidence to how much engineering effort a feature deserves. An experiment needs a different investment from a capability essential to the business. Early prototypes and watching people use them keep the feedback loop open after the initial idea has been validated. Audience questions explore hiring for product judgment, collaboration with product managers, and engineering responsibilities as teams grow. The first part establishes the discovery habits and technical ownership that guide the next stages of the workshop. items.title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Sandbox — Matt Brockman, E2B
items.excerpt: A runaway process consumes 99.7% of a sandbox's CPU, and killing it unlocks the next level of a capture the flag lab. Matt Brockman walks the room through deliberately broken environments to make sandbox operations concrete. Participants identify their sandbox, find memory pressure, locate a file filling the disk, and clean up background processes. Each challenge runs in its own environment, so a mistake can be reset without destroying the rest of the workshop. Brockman explains how E2B templates preserve a running system's state, including memory and the filesystem, so work can resume where it stopped. The exercises begin with Linux commands and configuration before moving into Python. The operational questions become harder when a few sandboxes turn into hundreds or thousands. A simulated lifecycle exercise gives a task enough time to finish, then shortens the idle timeout so unused resources do not keep consuming capacity. Another exercise replaces round robin assignment with a mapping from users to sandbox IDs, allowing each person to return to the same workspace. A cache example separates a template's readable files from the location that should receive runtime writes. Brockman also discusses the tradeoffs of restoring state: startup is convenient, but forgotten processes come back too. Audience questions cover volumes, storage growth, distributed workloads, orchestration, and network restrictions. The recurring task is keeping track of what runs where, what it can access, and when to clean it up. items.title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
items.excerpt: A customer support answer passes a test because it contains the word “cannot,” even though it approves a return outside the store's policy. Tejas Kumar builds that failure live to show where ordinary assertions and fuzzy matching stop being useful. The example grows into an LLM judge, then a dataset of customer scenarios, agent responses, and human verdicts. Along the way, the judge starts favoring an answer generated by its own model family. Adding the actual return policy improves its decisions, but missing details and a loyal customer's appeal still expose gaps. Kumar keeps examining disagreements, supplying context, and eventually changing the model rather than treating a green test as proof that the system works. The workshop connects those experiments to an evaluation process that can survive production. Test cases, expected behavior, a judge, and aggregation form the basic structure. Position bias, sycophancy, self preference, and verbosity can distort the result, so the instrument itself needs calibration. Kumar sets an 80% agreement threshold for a CI gate, then explains why fresh traffic and human review must keep the dataset current. An OpenRAG demonstration retrieves an uploaded refund policy instead of relying on a rule buried in a prompt. He also distinguishes checks performed before deployment from harness protections at runtime, and recommends starting with deterministic checks before paying for model judgments. Audience questions explore synthetic examples, shared policy, and where evaluation belongs in the development loop. items.title: Your AI Agent Is Confidently Wrong About Production — Willem Pienaar, Cleric
items.excerpt: Point an agent at a production alert and it comes back with a confident root cause. Often it's just the first error log it found. Willem Pienaar, co-founder and CTO of Cleric, explains why agents that are great at writing code struggle to debug production. Prod has no tests or linter to push back, it's sprawling, always changing and often impossible to reproduce, and LLMs are trained to be decisive when debugging needs doubt. He walks through the most common failure modes (mistaking a symptom for the cause, not knowing what's normal, lossy sub-agent summaries, anchoring on past incidents) and the grounding techniques that fix them. He also shows how tracking real outcomes after a fix lets you calibrate an agent's confidence so you can trust it. In this talk: • Why production debugging lacks the feedback loop coding has • Four failure modes: symptom vs cause, missing baselines, abstraction loss, anchoring • Grounding: parallel theories, baselines, dependency graphs, timing and evidence • Verifying fixes against real outcomes to calibrate confidence SPEAKER Willem Pienaar, Co-founder & CTO, Cleric LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/willempienaar/ X: https://x.com/willpienaar GitHub: https://github.com/woop LINKS Cleric: https://cleric.ai/ CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:13 Writing code isn't running it 0:38 The back-and-forth with agents 1:48 What we'll cover 2:12 Prod has no verification 2:57 Why prod is hard for agents 3:52 Models are trained to be confident 4:37 Common failure modes 5:02 Mistaking the symptom for the cause 5:32 Not knowing what's normal 5:47 The abstraction problem 6:11 Anchoring on past incidents 6:41 Techniques that work 7:11 Generate many theories 7:46 Compute a baseline 8:26 Use a dependency graph 9:06 Use time 9:35 Propagate the evidence 10:10 Results 1…
